uni-civil-building-materials.title: Building Materials & Construction
uni-civil-building-materials.description: The full first-level Building Materials syllabus of a civil degree: stones, bricks and blocks; lime and cement; aggregates and mortar; concrete; timber, steel, bitumen, paints and modern materials; plus standard laboratory practicals. Study companion; not a substitute for lab supervision.

lessons.title: Building stones: classification, properties and tests

story.title: Choosing a stone for a bridge pier

scenes.text: A contractor is offered cheap sandstone and costlier granite for a river-bridge pier.
The engineer asks for crushing strength, water absorption and an abrasion test before deciding.

steps.title: Classification and properties
steps.body:
**Geological:** igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone, limestone), metamorphic (marble, slate, quartzite).
**Physical:** stratified, unstratified, foliated.
**Good stone:** hard, tough, durable, non-porous, uniform, weather resistant, easily dressed. Typical crushing strength: granite 100–250 MPa, sandstone 20–100 MPa, marble 70–100 MPa. Specific gravity of most stones lies in 2.4–3.0. Water absorption after 24 h should be below about 5%.
**Tests:** crushing strength, water absorption, abrasion (Los Angeles / Deval), impact, hardness (Mohs), weathering, acid test for limestone.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 50 mm cube fails at 400 kN. Area = 2500 mm². Strength = 400000/2500 = **160 MPa** (granite range).

**Example 2.** Dry mass 1.20 kg, saturated 1.23 kg. Absorption = (1.23 − 1.20)/1.20 × 100 = **2.5 %**, acceptable.

**Example 3.** Apparent porosity: if absorbed water volume is 30 cm³ in a 1000 cm³ sample, n = 3 %.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using bed-parallel loading: stratified stones are weaker when loaded along the bedding planes; load them perpendicular to the bed.
- Dividing by the saturated mass instead of the dry mass for absorption.
- Forgetting kN→N conversion in crushing strength.

lessons.title: Bricks: raw materials, manufacture and classification

story.title: The brick kiln at the edge of town

scenes.text: A kiln owner wonders why one batch comes out pale and weak while another is deep red and ringing.
The answer lies in the clay mix, moulding and burning temperature.

steps.title: Constituents and process
steps.body:
**Clay composition:** alumina 20–30 % (plasticity), silica 50–60 % (shape, strength), lime < 5 % (fluxes silica; excess causes melting), iron oxide 5–6 % (colour, fluxing), magnesia (small, yellow tint), alkalies (excess causes efflorescence).
**Process:** excavation → weathering → tempering → moulding (hand or machine) → drying → burning at 900–1100 °C in clamp, Hoffmann or tunnel kiln.
**Classification (IS 1077):** by strength — 3.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5 … up to 40 MPa; first-class and second-class traditional grades; overburnt (jhama) bricks used as aggregate; underburnt are weak and absorb water.

steps.title: Standard sizes
steps.body: Modular brick: 190 × 90 × 90 mm (199 × 99 × 99 with mortar → nominal 200 × 100 × 100). Traditional: 230 × 110 × 70 mm. Unit weight of masonry ≈ 19 kN/m³.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Volume of 1 modular brick with mortar = 0.2 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.002 m³ → 500 bricks per m³ of masonry.

**Example 2.** Wall 10 m × 3 m × 0.2 m thick = 6 m³ → 3000 bricks (add ~5 % wastage = 3150).

**Example 3.** Excess lime in clay causes the brick to melt and distort in the kiln; excess alkalies → efflorescence (white salt patches).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting bricks using the size without mortar (190×90×90) — use the nominal size including mortar for quantity.
- Confusing silica (strength) with alumina (plasticity).
- Forgetting wastage.

scenes.text: A truck of bricks arrives. The site engineer takes 20 samples at random.
Compressive strength, water absorption and efflorescence tests decide whether the load is accepted.

steps.title: Field and lab tests
steps.body:
**Field:** uniform colour and size, metallic ringing sound when two bricks are struck, no scratch by thumbnail (hardness), fracture should be clean, a brick dropped from 1 m should not break.
**Lab:** compressive strength (frog filled with mortar, cured, loaded on bed area), water absorption (24 h cold immersion; Class designations typically ≤ 20 % for common bricks), efflorescence (nil to heavy), dimensions, warpage.
**Bonds:** stretcher bond (half-brick walls), header bond (curved walls), English bond (alternate courses of headers and stretchers — strongest), Flemish bond (headers and stretchers alternate in each course — better appearance). Queen closer ensures breaking of vertical joints; bats and closers fill gaps.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Load 420 kN on a 230 × 110 mm face: area = 25300 mm², σ = 420000/25300 = **16.6 MPa**.

**Example 2.** Dry 2.8 kg, after 24 h soak 3.2 kg: absorption = 0.4/2.8 × 100 = **14.3 %** (below 20 %).

**Example 3.** Average of 5 samples = 12.4, 11.8, 13.1, 12.0, 12.7 MPa → mean 12.4 MPa; classify as ≥ 12.5? No → class 10.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing wet bricks for compressive strength without stating the condition (strength drops when saturated).
- Using frog area instead of gross bed area.
- Believing Flemish bond is stronger than English; English is stronger, Flemish looks better.

lessons.title: Modern blocks: fly-ash, AAC, hollow and solid concrete

story.title: Why the new tower uses grey blocks

scenes.text: A high-rise needs lighter walls to cut dead load on columns.
The designer picks autoclaved aerated concrete (AAC) blocks over clay bricks.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
**Fly-ash bricks:** fly ash + lime + gypsum (or cement), cured not burnt; lower energy, uniform size; strength 7.5–12.5 MPa.
**AAC blocks:** cement, lime, fly ash/sand, aluminium powder; gas bubbles give density ≈ 550–700 kg/m³, good thermal insulation, light, cut easily; lower strength (3–4.5 MPa) and higher thinset-mortar need.
**Concrete blocks:** solid (≥ 75 % solid area) and hollow (<75 %, cavities up to 50 %); sizes e.g. 400×200×200 mm; hollow blocks reduce weight and improve insulation.
**CSEB (stabilised earth blocks):** soil + 5–8 % cement, compressed.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Wall 4 m × 3 m: area 12 m². One AAC block 600 × 200 mm face = 0.12 m² → 12/0.12 = **100 blocks**.

**Example 2.** Dead load saving: clay brick masonry 19 kN/m³ vs AAC 7 kN/m³. For 100 m³ of wall: (19 − 7) × 100 = **1200 kN** lighter.

**Example 3.** Density of hollow block: 18 kg mass, 400×200×200 = 0.016 m³ → 1125 kg/m³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ordinary cement–sand mortar on AAC (needs thin-bed adhesive or a compatible mortar).
- Treating a 7.5 MPa fly-ash brick like AAC strength.
- Ignoring that AAC must be protected from continuous wetting.

lessons.title: Lab: Brick compression and water-absorption test

scenes.text: Your batch of bricks has to be classified before a school building starts.
You record loads and weights, then compute the strength and absorption.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1. Select 5 bricks at random. 2. Measure L, B, H. 3. For absorption: oven-dry at 105–115 °C to constant mass W1; immerse in clean water 24 h at 27 ± 2 °C; wipe and weigh W2 within 3 min. 4. For strength: fill frog with 1:1 cement mortar, cure under damp jute 3 days, immerse 3 days, test on a CTM at 14 N/mm²/min.

steps.title: Observations (worked)
steps.body:
Brick 1: W1 = 3.10 kg, W2 = 3.52 kg → absorption 13.5 %. Failure load 380 kN on 230×110 mm (25300 mm²) → 15.0 MPa.
Average of 5 bricks = 14.6 MPa → can be rated as class 12.5 or better.

steps.title: Safety & errors
steps.body: Wear goggles; bricks shatter. Do not read the failure load after the needle drops. Record the mass quickly to avoid evaporation error.

scenes.text: A heritage architect insists the fort be re-plastered with lime, not cement.
Lime breathes, heals micro-cracks and matches the old masonry.

steps.title: Chemistry
steps.body:
**Calcination:** CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ at about 900 °C.
**Slaking:** CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat.
**Setting:** Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O (carbonation, slow).
**Types:** fat (high-calcium) lime — over 95 % CaO, slakes vigorously, no hydraulic set; hydraulic lime — has clay 5–30 %, sets under water; poor lime — more than 30 % clay/impurities, weak.
**Hydraulicity:** feebly (5–15 % clay), moderately (15–25 %), eminently (25–30 %).
**Uses:** plaster, masonry mortar, whitewash, soil stabilisation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1000 kg limestone (CaCO₃, 100 g/mol) yields CaO = 560 kg (56/100).

**Example 2.** 560 kg CaO slakes to 560 × 74/56 = **740 kg** Ca(OH)₂ (molar masses 56 → 74).

**Example 3.** Lime is chosen over cement for old brickwork because it is softer and more permeable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up calcination (heating) and slaking (water).
- Saying fat lime sets under water — only hydraulic lime does.
- Ignoring heat evolved during slaking (burn hazard).

lessons.title: Portland cement: manufacture and Bogue compounds

scenes.text: A 70 m rotary kiln turns slowly at 1450 °C, fusing limestone and clay into clinker.
The lab calculates compound percentages from oxide analysis.

steps.title: Process and compounds
steps.body:
**Raw materials:** limestone (CaO), clay/shale (SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃), gypsum (added 2–5 % to control flash set). **Dry process** is common (low fuel). Raw meal burnt to clinker at ≈ 1450 °C, cooled, ground with gypsum.
**Bogue compounds:** C₃S (alite, early strength, high heat), C₂S (belite, slow, long-term strength), C₃A (flash set, high heat, sulphate vulnerability), C₄AF (little strength, colour).
**Formulae (percent oxides):**
C₃S = 4.07C − 7.60S − 6.72A − 1.43F − 2.85SO₃
C₂S = 2.87S − 0.754C₃S
C₃A = 2.65A − 1.69F
C₄AF = 3.04F

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using formulae with oxide percent in decimals mixed with percent.
- Assuming high C₃S always = better: it raises heat of hydration and cracking risk.
- Dropping gypsum from the raw list.

lessons.title: Hydration, setting and types of cement

story.title: Cement for a dam and a deck

scenes.text: A dam's thick pour must not overheat; a deck slab must gain strength in a week.
Different cements are specified for each.

steps.title: Hydration and types
steps.body:
**Hydration:** C₃S + water → C–S–H gel + Ca(OH)₂ + heat. C–S–H gives strength. Heat of hydration ≈ 500 J/g in OPC.
**Grades of OPC (IS 269:2015):** 33, 43, 53 — 28-day mortar strength in MPa.
**Others:** PPC (fly ash 15–35 %), PSC (slag 25–70 %, resists sulphate, lower heat), rapid hardening (more C₃S, finer), low heat (limited C₃S/C₃A), sulphate-resisting (C₃A ≤ 5 %), white cement (low iron), high alumina (bauxite + limestone, fast, refractory), hydrophobic (water repellent film).
**Use:** mass concrete → PPC/PSC/low heat; marine/sulphate soils → SRC/PSC; precast → rapid hardening/OPC 53.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 28-day strength required 50 MPa mortar cube: use OPC 53 (≥ 53 MPa).

**Example 2.** Heat generated by 400 kg cement at 400 J/g: 400000 g × 400 J = 160 MJ per m³ of concrete.

**Example 3.** PPC vs OPC: PPC gains strength more slowly in 7 days but equals or exceeds OPC later, with better durability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the grade number as concrete grade: OPC 43 does NOT make M43 concrete.
- Using PSC where very early de-shuttering is needed.
- Confusing sulphate-resisting (low C3A) with low-heat (low C3S).

lessons.title: Testing cement: fineness, consistency, setting time, soundness, strength

scenes.text: Bags stored for months on a damp floor have lumps. The inspector orders tests.
Vicat apparatus and Le Chatelier moulds tell the truth.

steps.title: IS 4031 tests
steps.body:
**Fineness:** residue on 90 µm sieve ≤ 10 %; Blaine air-permeability ≥ 225 m²/kg (OPC).
**Standard consistency (P):** Vicat plunger penetrates to 5–7 mm from the bottom of the mould; P typically 26–33 %.
**Initial setting time:** water = 0.85 P; needle 1 mm² stops 5 ± 0.5 mm from the base; minimum **30 min**. **Final setting time:** annular attachment fails to make an impression; maximum **600 min** (OPC).
**Soundness:** Le Chatelier — expansion ≤ **10 mm**; autoclave ≤ 0.8 %.
**Compressive strength:** 70.6 mm cube, 1 : 3 cement : standard sand, water (P/4 + 3) % ; OPC 43 minimum 23, 33, 43 MPa at 3, 7, 28 days.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 400 g cement needs 112 mL for standard consistency: P = 112/400 = **28 %**.

**Example 2.** Water for initial setting time = 0.85 × 28 % × 400 g = **95.2 mL**.

**Example 3.** Le Chatelier: pointer separation 4 mm before, 11.5 mm after boiling → expansion 7.5 mm ≤ 10 mm: **sound**.

**Example 4.** Mortar cube fails at 120 kN, area 70.6² = 4984 mm² → 24.1 MPa at 3 days: passes OPC 43 (≥ 23).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 0.85P for the consistency test itself (it is for setting time).
- Computing the cube area with 70 mm instead of 70.6 mm.
- Testing lumpy cement without sieving the lumps — lumps mean partial hydration; reject if they do not break in the fingers.

lessons.title: Lab: Vicat apparatus — consistency and setting time

scenes.text: Four students share one Vicat apparatus and a stopwatch; every minute counts.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1. Weigh 400 g cement. 2. Mix with a trial water % for 3–5 min (gauging). 3. Fill the mould, level. 4. Lower the 10 mm plunger; read penetration. Repeat with new water % until penetration is 5–7 mm from the base. 5. For initial set, mix with 0.85P; start the clock when water is added; lower the needle every few minutes until it stays 5 ± 0.5 mm above the base.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body:
Trial 1: 26 % → 12 mm. Trial 2: 28 % → 8 mm. Trial 3: 30 % → 6 mm ✔. P = 30 %.
Initial set water = 0.85 × 30 = 25.5 % → 102 mL for 400 g.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Room 27 ± 2 °C, humidity ≥ 65 %. Vibration-free table. Never re-temper a mix.

scenes.text: A site replaces river sand with unwashed crusher dust and the concrete turns harsh.
Silt, shape and grading are the culprits.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body: Aggregates occupy 60–75 % of concrete volume. **Fine** passes 4.75 mm; **coarse** is retained on 4.75 mm. Grading zones for sand: I–IV (IS 383). **Shape:** rounded, irregular, angular, flaky, elongated. **Flakiness index** = % of particles with least dimension < 0.6 × mean size (thickness gauge); **elongation index** by length gauge. Specific gravity usually 2.6–2.7; bulk density 1500–1600 kg/m³ for coarse; water absorption < 2 % preferred. **Deleterious:** clay, silt (< 3–5 % in sand by IS 383), coal, shale, organic matter.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 800 g sample, particles passing the thickness gauge = 160 g → flakiness index = 160/800 = **20 %**.

**Example 2.** Aggregate Impact Value: 380 g sample, 60 g passes 2.36 mm → AIV = 60/380 × 100 = **15.8 %** (≤ 30 % for wearing surfaces, ≤ 45 % for concrete).

**Example 3.** Void ratio: bulk density 1550, particle density 2650 → voids = 1 − 1550/2650 = 41.5 %.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting higher AIV as 'better' — lower AIV means tougher aggregate.
- Using angularity to say strength drops: angular aggregate gives better bond but needs more paste.
- Ignoring organic impurities that retard hydration.

story.title: Grading curve at the batching plant

scenes.text: A plant technician plots cumulative percent passing on semi-log paper every morning.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Sieves: 80, 40, 20, 10, 4.75, 2.36, 1.18 mm, 600, 300, 150 µm. **Fineness Modulus** = Σ(cumulative % retained on the standard sieves)/100 (80 mm to 150 µm). FM sand 2.2–3.2 (fine 2.2–2.6, medium 2.6–2.9, coarse 2.9–3.2); coarse aggregate 5.5–8.0. Good grading → low voids → less paste.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cumulative % retained on 4.75, 2.36, 1.18, 600µ, 300µ, 150µ = 2, 12, 30, 55, 82, 96. Σ = 277 → **FM = 2.77** (medium sand).

**Example 2.** If two sands FM1 = 2.4 and FM2 = 3.0 are blended 50:50 by mass: FM = 2.7.

**Example 3.** Proportion x of sand A (FM 2.4) with B (FM 3.0) to get 2.6: x×2.4 + (1−x)×3.0 = 2.6 → x = 0.667.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Summing % passing instead of % retained.
- Including the pan fraction.
- Dividing by 10 rather than 100.

quiz.why: Zone I is coarsest, zone IV finest.

lessons.title: Bulking of sand and quantity adjustment

scenes.text: After rain, a pile of sand seems bigger than the same dry mass.
Volume batching on site must account for this.

steps.title: Concept
steps.body:
Surface moisture forms films that push grains apart, raising volume up to 20–40 % at 4–6 % moisture; fully dry or fully saturated sand shows no bulking.
**Test:** fill a cylinder with loose sand to height h₁; add water, stir, level: h₂. **Bulking % = (h₁ − h₂)/h₂ × 100** (equivalent volume).
**Correction:** actual bulked volume = dry volume × (1 + bulking). Increase sand for volume batching; weigh-batching avoids the issue.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** h₁ = 200 mm, h₂ = 160 mm → bulking = 40/160 × 100 = **25 %**.

**Example 2.** The mix needs 0.8 m³ of dry sand → bulked volume to batch = 0.8 × 1.25 = **1.0 m³**.

**Example 3.** 1:2:4 concrete, 10 bags: 10 × 0.035 = 0.35 m³ cement, 0.70 m³ dry sand, bulked at 20 %: 0.84 m³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying bulking to coarse aggregate (negligible).
- Dividing by h₁ instead of h₂.
- Forgetting that over-saturation removes bulking.

scenes.text: A rich 1:3 plaster cracks within a month on a ceiling.
A leaner mix and proper curing would have worked.

steps.title: Mortar proportions
steps.body: Mortar = binder + sand + water. Cement mortar: 1:3–1:6; lime mortar for old masonry; mixed (1:1:6) cement-lime. Dry volume ≈ 1.33 × wet volume of mortar (voids/shrinkage). **Water:** potable; pH ≥ 6; solids limits (IS 456): organic 200 mg/L, inorganic 3000, sulphate 400, chloride 2000 mg/L for plain concrete (500 for RCC). **Admixtures:** plasticizer, superplasticizer, retarder, accelerator, air-entraining, waterproofing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1 m³ of 1:4 mortar: dry vol = 1.33 m³. Cement = 1.33/5 = 0.266 m³ × 1440 kg/m³ = 383 kg = 7.66 bags; sand = 4 × 0.266 = 1.064 m³.

**Example 2.** Plaster 100 m² at 12 mm: wet volume = 1.2 m³; dry volume ≈ 1.6 m³ (wet ×1.33).

**Example 3.** Cement for 1:3 mortar, 0.5 m³ wet: dry = 0.665 m³; cement = 0.665/4 = 0.166 m³ = 239 kg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cement bag as 0.035 m³ and mixing with 1440 kg/m³ inconsistently.
- Rich mortar ≠ better: it shrinks and cracks.
- Using sea water in RCC (chloride corrodes steel).

steps.title: Workability
steps.body: Workability = ease of mixing, placing, compacting and finishing without segregation. **Factors:** water content, aggregate size/shape/grading, cement, admixtures, temperature, time. **Tests:** slump (IS 1199) — cone 300 mm high, 100 mm top, 200 mm bottom, 3 layers × 25 strokes; compaction factor (low-medium); Vee-Bee; flow table. **IS 456 slump ranges:** low 25–75, medium 50–100, high 100–150 mm. **Segregation:** separation of coarse from mortar; **bleeding:** water rising to the surface (reduces bond, laitance).

scenes.text: Cubes show 17 MPa at 7 days for M25. Panic? The engineer checks the 28-day expectation.

steps.title: Strength
steps.body: **Abrams' law:** f = A/B^(w/c). Lower w/c → denser paste, higher strength. Practical lower limit ≈ 0.25 (hydration needs ≈ 0.23–0.25 w/c). **IS 456 grades:** M10 … M80 (fck = char. 150 mm cube strength at 28 days, 5 % defective). **Relations:** flexural fcr = 0.7√fck; Ec = 5000√fck MPa; cylinder ≈ 0.8 cube. **Age:** ≈ 16 % at 1 d, 40 % 3 d, 65 % 7 d, 90 % 14 d, 99 % 28 d (OPC rule of thumb); 28-day strength is the reference.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 150 mm cube fails at 675 kN: 675000/22500 = **30 MPa**.

**Example 2.** M25: fcr = 0.7√25 = **3.5 MPa**; Ec = 5000√25 = **25000 MPa**.

**Example 3.** 7-day cube = 17 MPa. At ~65 % → 28-day ≈ 26 MPa → M25 likely OK (still wait for 28 d).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating M25 as 25 MPa mean (mean must be higher; target f'ck = fck + 1.65s).
- Using cylinder and cube strengths interchangeably.
- Judging by 7-day cubes.

courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A survey team maps a 50-acre site for a new college.
They first fix a framework of control points, then fill in detail — 'whole to part'.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body:
1. **Work from whole to part** — establish a control framework first so errors don't accumulate.
2. **Locate a new point by at least two independent measurements** from known points (distances, angles).
Classification: plane vs geodetic (curvature considered beyond ~250 km² areas); by instrument (chain, compass, plane table, theodolite, total station, GNSS); by purpose (topographic, cadastral, engineering, hydrographic).

steps.title: Errors
steps.body:
- **Mistakes/blunders** — carelessness; detect by checks.
- **Systematic** — follow a law (tape too long, temperature); can be corrected; cumulative.
- **Random (accidental)** — small, compensating; reduced by repetition; ∝ √n.
Precision ratio = error/distance (e.g. 1 in 5000).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 30 m tape found 0.05 m too long; measured distance 600 m ⇒ true = 600 × 30.05/30 = 601.0 m.

**Example 2.** Area measured with that tape as 4000 m² ⇒ true area = 4000 × (30.05/30)² = 4013.3 m².

**Example 3.** Random error 0.01 m per tape length, 20 lengths ⇒ probable total ≈ 0.01√20 = 0.045 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Correcting length with the ratio inverted (too long tape ⇒ true is longer).
- Area correction must use the square of the ratio.
- Treating systematic errors as compensating.

activity.prompt: A 20 m chain is 0.04 m too long. Measured 500 m. True length (m)?

quiz.why: The first principle of surveying is to work from the whole to the part: first fix a framework of major control points and then fill in the details inside it, which stops errors from building up.
Systematic errors follow a definite law (such as a wrong tape length) and have the same sign each time, so they accumulate rather than cancel.
options: follow a law and are cumulative

quiz.why: A tape that is too long covers more ground per tape length, so fewer lengths are needed and the measured length is shorter than the true length.
If the tape is wrongly long (L′ instead of L), lengths scale by L′/L and areas scale by the square, (L′/L)².
Random errors are as likely to be positive as negative, so they partly cancel and accumulate in proportion to the square root of the number of measurements, √n.

scenes.text: A baseline for a bridge survey must be accurate to 1 in 20 000.
Temperature, pull, sag and slope corrections all matter.

steps.title: Corrections
steps.body:
- **Absolute (standardisation):** C_a = L(c/l) (c = error per tape length l).
- **Temperature:** C_t = αL(T_m − T₀) (steel α ≈ 11.6×10⁻⁶/°C).
- **Pull:** C_p = (P − P₀)L/(AE).
- **Sag:** C_s = −W²L/(24P²) per span (W = tape weight in the span) — always negative.
- **Slope:** C_sl = −(L − √(L² − h²)) ≈ −h²/(2L) — always negative.
- **Normal tension:** pull at which pull and sag corrections cancel: P_n = 0.204W√(AE)/√(P_n − P₀).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 30 m steel tape standardised at 20 °C used at 35 °C: C_t = 11.6×10⁻⁶ × 30 × 15 = +5.2 mm per tape length.

**Example 2.** Sag: W = 6 N over a 30 m span with P = 100 N: C_s = −36 × 30/(24 × 10 000) = −4.5 mm.

**Example 3.** Slope: 30 m measured along a slope with 1.5 m height difference: C = −1.5²/60 = −0.0375 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign errors (sag and slope are always negative).
- Using total tape weight for spans that are shorter.
- Forgetting to convert E in N/mm² with A in mm².

activity.prompt: Slope correction (m) for 50 m measured on slope with 2 m rise (use −h²/2L).

quiz.why: A hanging tape forms a catenary, so the horizontal chord is shorter than the tape length. The sag correction is therefore always negative.
The temperature correction is C_t = αL(T_m − T₀), where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion and T₀ is the standardisation temperature.
At normal tension the elongation from the pull exactly balances the shortening due to sag, so the pull and sag corrections cancel.
By Hooke's law, the correction for pull is C_p = (P − P₀)L/(AE), based on the extra elongation of the tape.
A slope-measured length is longer than the horizontal distance, so the correction to get the horizontal length is negative.

scenes.text: A trekker reads 135° on a compass for the next ridge.
That is a whole-circle bearing; the map legend may show S 45° E.

steps.title: Systems
steps.body:
**Whole-circle bearing (WCB):** 0–360° clockwise from north (prismatic compass).
**Quadrantal (reduced) bearing (QB):** N θ E, S θ E, S θ W, N θ W (θ ≤ 90°, surveyor's compass).
Conversion: WCB 0–90 → N θ E; 90–180 → S (180 − θ) E; 180–270 → S (θ − 180) W; 270–360 → N (360 − θ) W.
Back bearing = FB ± 180°.
Included angle at a station = BB of previous line − FB of next line (adjust by 360° as needed).
Magnetic declination: true bearing = magnetic bearing ± declination (E positive).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** WCB 215° ⇒ S 35° W; back bearing 35°.

**Example 2.** FB of AB = 60°, FB of BC = 130°: BB of AB = 240°; angle ABC = 240 − 130 = 110°.

**Example 3.** Magnetic bearing 75°, declination 2° W ⇒ true bearing 73°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring QB from east/west instead of north/south.
- Forgetting ±180° for back bearings.
- Applying declination with the wrong sign.

activity.prompt: WCB → QB

quiz.why: The back bearing differs from the forward bearing by 180°. For 75° (< 180°) add 180°: 255°.
A WCB of 160° lies in the south-east quadrant (90°–180°), so QB = S (180° − 160°) E = S 20° E.

quiz.q: True bearing with magnetic 120°, declination 3° E
quiz.why: With east declination the magnetic north lies east of true north, so true bearing = magnetic bearing + declination = 120° + 3° = 123°.
A prismatic compass reads whole circle bearings (WCB) from 0° to 360°, while a surveyor's compass gives quadrantal bearings.

quiz.q: Included angle: BB of AB 250°, FB of BC 100°
quiz.why: Included angle = BB of AB − FB of BC = 250° − 100° = 150°.

scenes.text: Readings near a steel bridge differ from those taken elsewhere.
Local attraction from iron objects deflects the needle — it must be detected and corrected.

steps.title: Detection and correction
steps.body: Local attraction is present at a station if FB and BB of a line differ by ≠ 180°. Find a line whose FB and BB differ by exactly 180° — both its ends are free. Starting there, correct bearings of the next lines station by station (correction at a station applies to all bearings taken at that station). Alternatively, compute included angles (unaffected by local attraction at a station) and recompute bearings.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Traverse ABCD: AB FB 45°30′ BB 225°30′ (diff 180° ⇒ A, B free). BC FB 96°15′, BB 276°45′ (diff 180°30′). Since B is free, the correct BB of BC is 276°15′ ⇒ correction at C = −30′; then correct CD's FB at C by −30′ and continue.

**Example 2.** Closing error in a compass traverse: adjust graphically by Bowditch's rule (proportional to distance from the start).

steps.title: Plane table (brief)
steps.body: Methods: radiation, intersection, traversing, resection (three-point problem — Bessel's, trial-and-error). Plane-table surveys are quick for small-scale detail mapping.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying a station's correction to bearings taken elsewhere.
- Assuming included angles are affected by local attraction (they aren't).
- Starting correction from an affected station.

activity.prompt: Correcting local attraction
items: Tabulate FB and BB of all lines
Find a line whose FB and BB differ by exactly 180°
Treat its ends as free stations
Compute correction at the next station from the corrected back bearing
Apply that correction to all bearings observed at that station and continue

quiz.q: Local attraction is indicated when FB and BB differ by
quiz.why: If there is no local attraction, FB and BB of a line differ by exactly 180°. A different difference shows local attraction at one or both ends.
Local attraction deflects bearings read at one station by the same amount, so the differences between them (included angles) are free from this error.

quiz.q: Correction at a station applies to
quiz.why: The error caused by local attraction is the same for every bearing taken at that station, so the correction applies to all bearings from that station.
options: all bearings taken at that station

quiz.why: The three-point problem is solved in plane table surveying by resection, to locate the table's station from three known points.
Local attraction is caused by magnetic materials near the compass, such as iron poles, steel rails and cables with currents.

questions.why: In plane surveying the earth's surface is taken as a plane, so earth's curvature is ignored. This is acceptable for small areas.
Back bearing = fore bearing ± 180°. For 300° (> 180°) subtract 180°: 120°.
The sag correction is always negative, as the horizontal distance is less than the tape length.
A WCB of 250° is in the south-west quadrant. QB = S (250° − 180°) W = S 70° W.

questions.q: Temperature correction for 100 m at +20 °C over standard (α 11.6×10⁻⁶)
questions.why: C_t = αLΔT = 11.6 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 20 = 0.0232 m = +23.2 mm, positive since the temperature is above standard.

questions.q: True length: 30 m tape 0.03 m too short, measured 300 m
questions.why: A tape 0.03 m too short has true length 29.97 m, so 300 m measured is really 300 × 29.97/30 = 299.7 m.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Local attraction does not affect included angles at a station.  Reason (R): Both bearings at that station are deflected by the same amount.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: local attraction deflects all bearings at a station by the same amount, so the difference between two bearings (the included angle) is unchanged. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Sag correction: W = 8 N, L = 30 m, P = 80 N
Angle ABC with FB AB 30°, FB BC 110°
questions.why: BB of AB = 30° + 180° = 210°. Angle ABC = BB of AB − FB of BC = 210° − 110° = 100°.

questions.q: Pull correction: P − P₀ = 50 N, L = 30 m, A = 3 mm², E = 2×10⁵ N/mm²
Case: Line PQ has FB 152°30′ and BB 333°00′. Station P is free. Correction at Q
questions.why: FB of PQ is 152°30′, so the true BB should be 332°30′. The observed 333°00′ is too large by 30′, so the correction at Q is −30′.

questions.q: Magnetic bearing 210°, declination 4° W: true bearing
questions.why: A west declination means magnetic north lies west of true north, so true bearing = magnetic − declination = 210° − 4° = 206°.

questions.q: Area plotted with a 20 m chain 0.08 m too long: measured 2.5 ha ⇒ true
questions.why: A chain that is too long makes measured values too small, so the area is under-measured. True area = 2.5 × (20.08/20)² ≈ 2.5 × 1.008 ≈ 2.52 ha.

questions.q: Slope 8° over 100 m measured length: horizontal correction
questions.why: The horizontal distance is 100 cos 8° = 99.027 m, so the correction is 100(1 − cos 8°) ≈ −0.973 m.

questions.q: Precision of 0.05 m error over 400 m
questions.why: The precision is the error divided by the length: 0.05/400 = 1/8000.

courses.title: Surveying · Unit 2 · Levelling and contouring
courses.summary: Levelling terms and instruments, temporary adjustments, height-of-instrument and rise-and-fall methods with arithmetic checks, curvature and refraction, reciprocal levelling, sensitivity of bubble tube, contours, their characteristics and uses.
outcomes: Reduce levels by HI and rise-and-fall methods with checks
Apply curvature and refraction corrections
Use reciprocal levelling to eliminate instrument errors
Interpret and use contour maps
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Levelling terms and the HI method

scenes.text: A road must fall 1 in 200 to drain rainwater.
Levelling gives the reduced level (RL) of every point.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: Benchmark (BM, known RL); backsight (BS — first reading after setting up, on a known point); foresight (FS — last reading before shifting); intermediate sight (IS); change point (CP, both FS and BS); height of instrument HI = RL + BS.

steps.title: HI (height of collimation) method
steps.body:
HI = RL(BM) + BS; RL = HI − FS (or IS). New HI at each set-up = RL(CP) + BS.
Check: ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL (intermediate sights are not checked).
Temporary adjustments: setting up, levelling up (bubble central), elimination of parallax.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** BM RL 100.000, BS 1.250 ⇒ HI 101.250. IS 2.100 ⇒ RL 99.150. FS (CP) 0.950 ⇒ RL 100.300. New BS 1.800 ⇒ HI 102.100. FS 2.400 ⇒ RL 99.700.
Check: ΣBS = 3.050, ΣFS = 3.350 ⇒ difference −0.300 = 99.700 − 100.000 ✔

**Example 2.** Gradient between points 50 m apart with RL difference 0.25 m = 1 in 200.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including IS in the arithmetic check sums.
- Using HI from the previous set-up after shifting the instrument.
- Reading the staff upside-down or with parallax.

activity.prompt: BM RL 50.000, BS 1.625. FS on point P = 2.875. RL of P?

quiz.why: By the height of instrument (collimation) method, HI = RL of the point + backsight (BS).

quiz.q: First reading after setting up on a known point
quiz.why: The first staff reading taken after setting up on a point of known RL is the backsight.
The check for the HI method is ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL.
options: ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL

quiz.why: A change point is where the instrument is moved: a foresight is taken on it from the old set-up and a backsight from the new one.
Parallax is removed by focusing the eyepiece for cross-hair sharpness and then the objective for the staff image.

scenes.text: For a long levelling line, the engineer wants a check on intermediate sights too.
Rise-and-fall checks every reading, unlike the HI method.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Rise/fall = previous reading − current reading (positive = rise). RL = previous RL + rise (or − fall).
Checks: ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL (all readings including IS are checked).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Readings: BS 1.200 (BM 100.000), IS 1.850, IS 0.950, FS 1.450.
1.200 → 1.850: fall 0.650 ⇒ 99.350; 1.850 → 0.950: rise 0.900 ⇒ 100.250; 0.950 → 1.450: fall 0.500 ⇒ 99.750.
Check: ΣBS − ΣFS = −0.250; ΣR − ΣF = 0.900 − 1.150 = −0.250; last − first = −0.250 ✔

**Example 2.** Comparison: HI method is quicker for many IS (profiles, contouring); rise-and-fall is more accurate (complete checks).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign of rise/fall (previous minus current).
- Skipping a check column.
- Computing rise/fall across a change point incorrectly (use FS at CP vs previous, then new BS starts fresh).

activity.prompt: Which method?

quiz.why: If the current staff reading is less than the previous reading, the ground has risen, so there is a rise.
The rise-and-fall method compares each pair of consecutive readings, so every reading, including intermediate sights, is checked.
The reading increased from 1.4 to 2.1, so the staff is on lower ground: previous − current = 1.4 − 2.1 = −0.7, a fall of 0.7.
The arithmetic check is ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL.
The HI method needs fewer calculations, especially with many intermediate sights, so it is faster for long profiles.

scenes.text: A team must carry levels across a 500 m wide river — the instrument can't be set midway.
Reciprocal levelling cancels curvature, refraction and collimation errors.

steps.title: Corrections (d in km)
steps.body:
Curvature C_c = −0.0785d² m; refraction C_r = +0.0112d² m (≈ 1/7 of curvature); combined C = −0.0673d² m (staff reading too large).
Distance to visible horizon: d = 3.855√h km (combined, h in m).
Reciprocal levelling: true difference H = ½[(h_a1 − h_b1) + (h_a2 − h_b2)], where readings are taken with the instrument near A then near B; error e = ½[(h_a1 − h_b1) − (h_a2 − h_b2)].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sight of 1.5 km: combined correction = −0.0673 × 2.25 = −0.151 m.

**Example 2.** Reciprocal: near A: A 1.025, B 1.630; near B: A 0.825, B 1.360. H = ½[(−0.605) + (−0.535)] = −0.570 ⇒ B is 0.570 m lower than A. Error = ½(−0.605 + 0.535) = −0.035 m.

**Example 3.** Observer eye 1.6 m above sea: horizon at 3.855√1.6 = 4.88 km.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using d in metres in 0.0673d².
- Sign: corrections are subtracted from staff readings.
- Taking a single set of readings across a river (errors don't cancel).

activity.prompt: Combined curvature–refraction correction for a 2 km sight (m, magnitude)?

quiz.why: The curvature correction is C_c = 0.0785d² metres with d in km (equal to d²/2R).
The refraction correction is about 1/7 of the curvature correction and has the opposite sign, so the combined correction is 0.0673d².
By reciprocal levelling, readings taken from both ends and averaged cancel collimation error and the effects of curvature and refraction.

quiz.q: Combined correction sign on staff reading
quiz.why: Curvature makes the staff reading too large, so the combined curvature and refraction correction is subtracted from the reading.
Distance to the horizon d = 3.855√h km. For h = 4 m, d = 3.855 × 2 ≈ 7.71 km.

scenes.text: Engineers estimate how much water a valley can hold using a contour map.
Contour lines join points of equal elevation.

steps.title: Characteristics
steps.body:
- Contour interval (CI) constant on a map; horizontal equivalent = horizontal distance between adjacent contours.
- Close contours ⇒ steep slope; widely spaced ⇒ gentle; equally spaced ⇒ uniform slope.
- Contours never cross except at overhangs; they close on themselves (within or beyond the map).
- V-shapes pointing uphill ⇒ valley; pointing downhill ⇒ ridge.
- Contours cross ridge/valley lines at right angles.

steps.title: Methods and uses
steps.body:
Direct (locate points on a contour) or indirect (grid/cross-section spot levels + interpolation). Uses: route location (constant gradient), intervisibility, catchment and reservoir capacity, earthwork volumes, site grading.
Reservoir capacity (trapezoidal): V = h[(A₁ + A_n)/2 + A₂ + … + A_(n−1)]; prismoidal: V = (h/3)[A₁ + A_n + 4ΣA_even + 2ΣA_odd].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** CI 2 m, horizontal equivalent 40 m ⇒ slope 1 in 20.

**Example 2.** Areas within contours 100, 102, 104 m: 2000, 3000, 4500 m². Trapezoidal V = 2[(2000 + 4500)/2 + 3000] = 12 500 m³; prismoidal V = (2/3)(2000 + 4500 + 12 000) = 12 333 m³.

**Example 3.** Interpolation: points 98.4 and 101.2 m are 28 m apart ⇒ the 100 m contour lies 16 m from the first point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Misreading ridges as valleys.
- Using Simpson's (prismoidal) rule with an even number of areas.
- Treating CI as variable on one map.

activity.prompt: Contour interval 5 m, horizontal equivalent 100 m. Slope as '1 in ___'?

quiz.why: Contours close together mean the ground rises quickly over a short horizontal distance, which indicates a steep slope.
Contours cross ridge lines (and valley lines) at right angles.
V-shaped contours with the V pointing toward higher ground represent a valley, with the stream running down the middle. A ridge shows V's pointing downhill.
Contours at different elevations cannot cross except at an overhanging cliff or cave, where one lies directly above the other.
Reservoir capacity is found by finding the areas enclosed by successive contours and applying the trapezoidal or prismoidal formula.

questions.why: A benchmark is a fixed point whose RL (reduced level) is known and is used as the reference in levelling.
RL of a point = height of instrument (HI) − staff reading on that point.
The contour interval is the constant vertical distance between successive contour lines.
C_c = 0.0785d² with d = 1 km is 0.0785 m.

questions.q: Gradient: RL difference 1.2 m over 240 m
questions.why: Gradient = horizontal distance/vertical difference = 240/1.2 = 200, i.e. 1 in 200.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Rise-and-fall method gives a check on intermediate sights.  Reason (R): ΣRise − ΣFall must equal ΣBS − ΣFS, which involves every reading.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: the rise-and-fall method works out the level change between each pair of consecutive readings, so every reading including IS enters. The check ΣRise − ΣFall = ΣBS − ΣFS therefore covers them, and the reason explains the assertion.
The true difference of level is the mean of the two apparent differences: (−0.80 − 0.70)/2 = −0.75 m, so B is lower than A by 0.75 m.

questions.q: Readings 2.4, 1.6, 2.9 from BM 200.000 (BS 2.4): RL of last point
questions.why: HI = 200.000 + 2.4 = 202.4. The next readings are 1.6 (RL 200.8) and 2.9 (RL 199.5), so the last point is at 199.5.

questions.q: Prismoidal volume: h 3 m, areas 1000, 1600, 2400 m²
Case: A lighthouse 36 m high is visible to a ship whose observer is 4 m above sea. Max distance
questions.why: Distance to horizon d = 3.855√h km. The sum is 3.855(√36 + √4) = 3.855 × 8 ≈ 30.8 km.
The combined correction is 0.0673d² = 0.0673 × 3² = 0.0673 × 9 ≈ 0.606 m, subtractive.

questions.q: Interpolate 50 m contour between 47.5 m and 52.5 m spaced 40 m
questions.why: The 50 m contour lies 2.5 m above 47.5 m out of a total difference of 5 m, so it lies (2.5/5) × 40 = 20 m from the first point.

questions.q: Sensitivity of bubble: staff reading change 0.02 m at 100 m for 2 divisions
questions.why: The tilt per division is the change in reading/distance: 0.02/(2 × 100) = 10⁻⁴ rad = 10⁻⁴ × 206265″ ≈ 20.6″.

questions.q: Collimation error per 100 m from reciprocal error −0.035 m over 500 m
questions.why: The error is proportional to distance. −0.035 m over 500 m is −0.035/5 = −0.007 m per 100 m.

courses.title: Surveying · Unit 3 · Theodolite, traversing, areas and tacheometry
courses.summary: Theodolite parts, temporary adjustments and measurement of horizontal and vertical angles (repetition, reiteration), theodolite traversing with latitudes and departures, closing error and Bowditch/transit adjustment, area by coordinates, and stadia tacheometry.
outcomes: Measure horizontal and vertical angles with face-left/face-right
Compute latitudes, departures and closing error
Adjust a traverse with Bowditch's rule and compute area by coordinates
Apply the stadia formula for distance and elevation
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A site engineer sets out a 90° corner for a building foundation.
A theodolite measures angles to seconds of arc.

steps.title: Instrument and adjustments
steps.body:
Parts: tribrach, levelling screws, lower and upper plates, telescope, vertical circle, plate bubble, vernier/digital readouts. Temporary adjustments: centring, levelling, focusing (eyepiece then objective).
Terms: face left/face right (FL/FR), transiting (plunging), swinging.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Repetition method:** angle accumulated n times and divided — reduces reading errors.
**Reiteration (direction method):** several angles measured from one station by sighting stations in turn and closing the horizon (sum = 360°).
Taking FL and FR readings and averaging eliminates collimation, horizontal axis and index errors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Repetition 6 times: initial 0°00′00″, final 261°31′30″ ⇒ angle = 43°35′15″.

**Example 2.** FL 35°20′20″, FR 35°20′40″ ⇒ mean 35°20′30″.

**Example 3.** Vertical angle: FL +12°30′, FR +12°32′ ⇒ mean 12°31′, index error ±1′.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add 360° multiples when the reading passes zero in repetition.
- Using only one face.
- Disturbing the lower clamp between repetitions.

activity.prompt: Repetition 4 times: final reading 182°06′00″ from 0°. Mean angle in decimal degrees?

quiz.why: Averaging face-left and face-right readings cancels instrumental errors such as line of collimation error and horizontal (trunnion) axis error. Centring errors are not removed.
The reiteration method, also called the direction method, measures several angles from a common reference line and is used for many stations.
Repetition is used to measure the same angle several times by accumulating it on the circle, so the reading error is divided among the repeats and precision increases.
Transiting (plunging) is turning the telescope through 180° about its horizontal axis to change face.
options: rotating the telescope about the horizontal axis

quiz.q: Sum of angles closing the horizon
quiz.why: The angles measured around a point to close the horizon add to 360°, which is used to check the work.

scenes.text: A surveyor runs a closed traverse around a farm boundary.
Latitudes and departures must sum to zero — otherwise there's a closing error.

steps.title: Computations
steps.body:
Latitude L = l cos θ (N +, S −), departure D = l sin θ (E +, W −) (θ = WCB or reduced bearing with signs).
Closed traverse: ΣL = 0, ΣD = 0 ideally. Closing error e = √((ΣL)² + (ΣD)²), direction tan⁻¹(ΣD/ΣL). Relative precision = e/perimeter.
Angular check: sum of interior angles = (2n − 4) × 90°.
**Bowditch rule** (angles and distances equally precise): correction to L of a line = −ΣL × (l/Σl); same for D.
**Transit rule:** correction ∝ |L|/Σ|L| (angles more precise).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Line 200 m at WCB 30°: L = 173.21 N, D = 100.00 E.

**Example 2.** Traverse perimeter 1000 m with ΣL = +0.30, ΣD = −0.40: e = 0.50 m ⇒ precision 1 in 2000. A 250 m line gets corrections ΔL = −0.075, ΔD = +0.100.

**Example 3.** Pentagon: interior angles should sum to (10 − 4) × 90 = 540°.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Signs of latitude/departure from QB quadrants.
- Applying corrections with the same sign as the error.
- Using Bowditch when angles are much more precise than distances (transit rule fits better).

activity.prompt: Closing error: ΣL = 0.6 m, ΣD = 0.8 m. Error magnitude (m)?

quiz.why: Latitude is the projection of a line on the north–south axis, l cos θ. Departure is l sin θ.

quiz.q: Interior angle sum of a hexagon
quiz.why: Interior angles of a closed n-sided traverse add to (2n − 4) × 90°. For a hexagon (n = 6) that is 8 × 90° = 720°.
Bowditch's rule distributes the closing error to each latitude and departure in proportion to the length of the line.

quiz.q: Departure of 100 m line at WCB 270°
quiz.why: A WCB of 270° is due west, so the line lies wholly along the E–W axis and has a departure of −100 m (west is negative).
Relative precision of a traverse is the closing error divided by the total perimeter, usually written as 1 in N.

lessons.title: Area by coordinates and other methods

scenes.text: Property areas in land records are computed from boundary coordinates.
The coordinate (shoelace) formula does it exactly for straight-sided plots.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Coordinates (shoelace):** A = ½|Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)|.
**Offsets from a baseline (irregular boundary):** trapezoidal A = d[(O₁ + O_n)/2 + O₂ + … + O_(n−1)]; Simpson's A = (d/3)[O₁ + O_n + 4Σeven + 2Σodd] (odd number of offsets).
Planimeter for maps. Double meridian distance (DMD) method also used for traverses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not closing the coordinate list back to the first point.
- Using Simpson's rule with an even number of offsets.
- Sign (take the absolute value).

activity.prompt: Area of triangle with vertices (0,0), (40,0), (0,30) by coordinates (m²)?

quiz.why: The shoelace (coordinate) formula is Area = ½|Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)|, using the coordinates of the vertices.
Simpson's rule treats strips in pairs, so it needs an odd number of offsets (an even number of strips).
One hectare is defined as 10,000 m² (100 m × 100 m).
Trapezoidal rule: Area = (d/2)[first + last + 2 × others] = (10/2)[0 + 0 + 2 × 6] = 60 m². (Equivalent to 10 × (0 + 6).)
A planimeter is the instrument used to measure the area of a figure on a map or plan by tracing its outline.

scenes.text: Surveying hilly terrain with tapes would take weeks.
Tacheometry gets distance and height from one staff reading set.

steps.title: Stadia formulas
steps.body:
Horizontal sight: D = kS + C (k = f/i, usually 100; C = f + d, ≈ 0 for anallactic/internal-focusing telescopes); S = staff intercept (top − bottom hair).
Inclined sight (staff vertical), angle θ: D = kS cos²θ + C cos θ; V = kS sin 2θ/2 + C sin θ.
RL of staff point = HI + V − h (h = middle hair reading) (for elevation).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Horizontal sight, k = 100, C = 0, readings 1.250/1.625/2.000: S = 0.750 ⇒ D = 75 m.

**Example 2.** θ = +8°, S = 1.200, middle 1.800, HI 100.50: D = 120 cos²8° = 117.68 m; V = 60 sin 16° = 16.54 m; RL = 100.50 + 16.54 − 1.80 = 115.24 m.

**Example 3.** Determining k: staff intercepts 0.5 and 1.0 m at known 50 and 100 m ⇒ k = 100, C = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cos θ instead of cos²θ for horizontal distance.
- Forgetting to subtract the middle-hair reading for elevations.
- Holding the staff not vertical (use the right formula).

activity.prompt: Stadia: k = 100, C = 0, intercept 0.86 m, horizontal sight. Distance (m)?

quiz.why: For a horizontal sight in stadia tacheometry, the horizontal distance is D = kS + C, where k is the multiplying constant, S the staff intercept and C the additive constant.
Stadia instruments are made with a multiplying constant k = f/i = 100.
For inclined sights with the staff held vertical, the horizontal distance is D = kS cos²θ (+ C cos θ).
An anallactic lens makes the additive constant C ≈ 0, so the distance is simply proportional to the staff intercept.

questions.why: A theodolite is used to measure both horizontal and vertical angles. It is more accurate than a compass.
Departure is the projection of a traverse line on the east–west axis: l sin θ. Latitude is l cos θ.
Simpson's one-third rule takes strips in pairs, so it needs an odd number of ordinates (an even number of strips).
For a closed traverse the interior angles add to (2n − 4) × 90°. For a quadrilateral n = 4, so (8 − 4) × 90° = 360°.
Latitude = l cos θ = 150 cos 120° = 150 × (−0.5) = −75 m, since 120° points south.
For a horizontal sight, D = kS + C = 100 × 1.45 + 0.3 = 145 + 0.3 = 145.3 m.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Averaging face-left and face-right readings eliminates collimation error.  Reason (R): The error has equal magnitude and opposite sign on the two faces.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: the collimation error has equal size but opposite sign on the two faces, so the mean of face-left and face-right readings cancels it. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Closing error ΣL = −0.12, ΣD = 0.16 over 2000 m: precision
questions.why: Linear closing error e = √(0.12² + 0.16²) = 0.20 m. Precision = e/perimeter = 0.2/2000 = 1/10,000.
The points form a parallelogram with base 50 m and height 40 m, so area = 50 × 40 = 2000 m². The shoelace formula gives the same.

questions.q: Bowditch correction to latitude of a 300 m line: ΣL = +0.45, perimeter 1500 m
questions.why: Bowditch: correction = −(ΣL) × (line length/perimeter) = −0.45 × 300/1500 = −0.09 m. It is opposite to the sign of the error.

questions.q: Case: Tacheometer at HI 210.30 sights staff at θ = −6°, S = 0.95, middle 1.40 (k 100, C 0). RL of staff point
questions.why: D = kS cos²θ, V = (kS/2) sin 2θ = 47.5 × sin 12° ≈ 9.88 m. The line of sight is depressed, so RL = HI − V − middle reading = 210.30 − 9.88 − 1.40 ≈ 199.02 m.
Horizontal distance D = kS cos²θ = 95 × cos²6° = 95 × 0.989 ≈ 93.96 m.

questions.q: Simpson's area with offsets 2, 4, 6, 4, 2 m at 5 m
Repetition 8 times final reading 2°40′00″ after passing zero once (angle ≈ 45°)
questions.why: The accumulated reading after passing zero once is 360° + 2°40′ = 362°40′. Dividing by 8 repetitions gives 45°20′.

questions.q: Transit rule distributes corrections in proportion to
questions.why: The transit rule distributes the closing error to latitudes and departures in proportion to the size of the latitudes and departures themselves. (Bowditch uses line lengths.)

courses.title: Surveying · Unit 4 · Curves and modern surveying (total station, GNSS, remote sensing, GIS)
courses.summary: Simple circular curves (elements, degree of curve, chainages), setting out by offsets and Rankine's deflection-angle method, transition curves and their length, total station operation and errors, GNSS principles and accuracy, remote sensing and GIS basics.
outcomes: Compute elements and chainages of a simple circular curve
Set out curves by Rankine's deflection angles
Explain total station and GNSS (including RTK) surveying
Describe remote-sensing data and GIS layers for engineering use
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Two straight highway sections meet at an intersection point at 40°.
A circular curve of radius 400 m joins them smoothly.

steps.title: Elements (deflection angle Δ, radius R)
steps.body:
Tangent length T = R tan(Δ/2); curve length L = πRΔ/180; long chord = 2R sin(Δ/2); external distance E = R(sec(Δ/2) − 1); mid-ordinate M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2)).
Degree of curve (30 m arc): D = 1718.9/R (degrees); (20 m arc: 1146/R).
Chainage of T₁ = chainage of PI − T; chainage of T₂ = T₁ + L.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Δ = 40°, R = 400 m: T = 400 tan 20° = 145.59 m; L = 279.25 m; long chord = 273.62 m; E = 25.67 m; M = 24.12 m.

**Example 2.** PI at chainage 1200.00 m: T₁ at 1054.41 m; T₂ at 1333.66 m.

**Example 3.** R = 573 m ⇒ D ≈ 3° (30 m arc).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Δ instead of Δ/2 in tangent length.
- Chainage of T₂ = PI + T (wrong — use T₁ + curve length).
- Degrees vs radians in L.

activity.prompt: Simple curve R = 300 m, Δ = 60°. Tangent length (m, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The tangent length of a simple circular curve is T = R tan(Δ/2), where Δ is the deflection angle.
The curve length is the arc: L = πRΔ/180 with Δ in degrees.
The long chord joins the two tangent points: 2R sin(Δ/2).
The chainage of the end tangent point T₂ is the chainage of T₁ plus the curve length (measured along the curve), not the tangent length.

quiz.q: Degree of curve (30 m) for R = 1719 m
quiz.why: For a 30 m chord, degree of curve D ≈ 1718.9/R. With R = 1719, D ≈ 1°.

lessons.title: Setting out curves: offsets and Rankine's method

scenes.text: Pegs must be placed every 20 m along the curve on site.
Rankine's deflection angles from T₁ let one theodolite do it.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Linear (offsets):** from the long chord: O_x = √(R² − x²) − (R − M); from tangents: O_x ≈ x²/(2R).
**Rankine's (tangential angles):** deflection for a chord c: δ (minutes) = 1718.9 c/R; total deflection Δₙ = Σδ. Initial sub-chord to reach a round chainage, normal chords, final sub-chord.
**Two-theodolite method** and total-station coordinate method for precision.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** R = 400 m, normal chord 20 m: δ = 1718.9 × 20/400 = 85.9′ = 1°25′57″.

**Example 2.** T₁ at 1054.41 ⇒ first sub-chord to 1060 = 5.59 m: δ₁ = 1718.9 × 5.59/400 = 24.0′.

**Example 3.** Tangent offset at 60 m from T₁ for R = 400: ≈ 3600/800 = 4.5 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting sub-chords at the start/end.
- Using full chord deflection for a sub-chord.
- Not checking final total deflection equals Δ/2.

activity.prompt: Rankine's method on site
items: Compute chainages of T₁ and T₂
Compute initial sub-chord, normal chords and final sub-chord
Compute deflection angles and cumulative totals
Set theodolite at T₁ sighting the PI and set each total deflection
Measure chords from the previous peg to locate each peg; check last total = Δ/2

quiz.why: Rankine's deflection angle for a chord c is δ = (1718.9 c/R) minutes, i.e. half the central angle subtended by the chord.
The total deflection angle to T₂ from T₁ equals half of the deflection angle of the curve, Δ/2, which serves as a check.
The offset from the tangent at distance x is approximately y = x²/(2R) for small x, from the circle's equation.

quiz.q: Deflection for 30 m chord, R = 600 m

quiz.why: Modern practice sets out curves with a total station using coordinates, which is fast and precise, instead of chain-and-tape methods.

scenes.text: Drivers don't feel a jerk entering expressway curves.
A transition (spiral) curve gradually raises curvature and superelevation.

steps.title: Transition curves
steps.body:
Ideal: clothoid (radius ∝ 1/length). Length by rate of change of centripetal acceleration: L = v³/(C R) (C ≈ 0.3–0.8 m/s³; IRC uses C = 80/(75 + V) with V in km/h). Shift S = L²/(24R).
Also cubic parabola used for railways and highways; vertical curves are parabolic (sag/summit).

steps.title: Total station
steps.body: Combines electronic theodolite + EDM + microprocessor/data logger: measures horizontal/vertical angles and slope distance, computes coordinates and elevations. EDM by phase comparison (infrared/laser); reflectorless mode for inaccessible points. Corrections: prism constant, atmospheric (temperature/pressure ppm), curvature/refraction. Accuracy e.g. ±(2 mm + 2 ppm).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V = 80 km/h (22.2 m/s), R = 300 m, C = 0.5: L = 22.2³/(0.5 × 300) = 73 m; shift = 73²/(24 × 300) = 0.74 m.

**Example 2.** Total station: slope distance 250.000 m at zenith angle 85°: horizontal = 249.049 m; vertical = 21.789 m.

**Example 3.** ±(2 mm + 2 ppm) over 1 km ⇒ ±4 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V in km/h in v³ (convert to m/s).
- Forgetting the prism constant.
- Using vertical angle formulas with zenith angles (sin/cos swap).

activity.prompt: Total station: slope distance 100 m, zenith angle 80°. Horizontal distance (m, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: An ideal transition curve has curvature increasing linearly with length, which is a clothoid (Euler spiral). A cubic parabola is a close approximation.
The shift of a transition curve is s = L²/(24R), the distance the main circular curve moves inwards.
A total station is an electronic theodolite with an EDM, so it measures both angles and distances.

quiz.q: EDM accuracy ±(2 mm + 2 ppm) at 2 km
quiz.why: Total error = 2 mm + 2 ppm × 2 km = 2 mm + 4 mm = ±6 mm (1 ppm is 1 mm per km).
The length of a transition curve from the rate of change of radial acceleration is L = v³/(CR), where C is the rate of change of acceleration.

scenes.text: A smart-city project uses drones, satellites and GIS to map every road and pipe.
GNSS gives positions; remote sensing gives images; GIS organises it all.

steps.title: GNSS
steps.body: Constellations: GPS (USA), GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, and India's NavIC (IRNSS) regional system. Position from pseudoranges to ≥ 4 satellites (x, y, z, clock bias). Errors: satellite clock/orbit, ionospheric and tropospheric delays, multipath, geometry (DOP). Accuracy: standalone metres; DGPS sub-metre; **RTK** centimetre-level using a base station or network corrections (CORS); static post-processing millimetres–centimetres.

steps.title: Remote sensing and GIS
steps.body:
Remote sensing: passive (optical/multispectral, thermal) and active (radar/SAR, LiDAR) sensors; resolution — spatial, spectral, radiometric, temporal. Indices such as NDVI = (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red) for vegetation. Indian Earth-observation satellites (e.g. Cartosat, Resourcesat) provide data.
GIS: layers of vector (points, lines, polygons) and raster data with attributes; overlay, buffer, network and terrain analysis (DEM, slope). Uses: route alignment, flood mapping, land use, utility management.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** NDVI with NIR = 0.5, Red = 0.1: (0.4)/(0.6) = 0.67 ⇒ healthy vegetation.

**Example 2.** A 100 m buffer around a river in GIS identifies plots needing flood clearance.

**Example 3.** RTK rover 5 km from base ⇒ typically ~1–2 cm horizontal accuracy (open sky).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting centimetre accuracy from a phone GPS.
- Ignoring datum/coordinate-system differences (WGS84 vs local).
- Mixing raster resolution with map scale.

activity.prompt: Technology → use

quiz.why: GNSS needs 4 satellites for a 3-D fix: three unknown coordinates plus the receiver clock error, which gives four unknowns.
NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation, earlier IRNSS) is India's regional satellite navigation system.
NDVI = (NIR − Red)/(NIR + Red). Healthy vegetation reflects strongly in near-infrared, giving high values.
An active sensor emits its own energy and measures the return, as radar and LiDAR do. Cameras in sunlight are passive.
Vector GIS data consists of points, lines and polygons. Pixels are raster data.

questions.why: A total station combines an electronic theodolite with an electronic distance meter (EDM) and a microprocessor.
A 3-D position needs 4 satellites: three for position and one to correct the receiver clock.

questions.q: Degree of curve (30 m) for R = 860 m
Assertion (A): RTK GNSS achieves centimetre accuracy.  Reason (R): It uses carrier-phase corrections from a nearby base station.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: RTK applies carrier-phase corrections from a nearby base station, removing most of the common errors, which gives centimetre accuracy. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Rankine δ for 10 m sub-chord, R = 250
Transition length: v = 25 m/s, R = 500 m, C = 0.5
Case: PI at chainage 2500 m, Δ = 50°, R = 300 m. Chainage of T₂
Horizontal distance: slope 300 m, vertical angle +10°
questions.why: Horizontal distance = slope length × cos(vertical angle) = 300 cos 10° ≈ 295.44 m.

questions.q: Shift for L = 80 m, R = 400 m
Final check in Rankine's method: total deflection at T₂ for Δ = 50°
questions.why: As a check in Rankine's method, the final total deflection at T₂ must equal Δ/2 = 25°.

steps.title: Tapes and compass
steps.body:

steps.title: How to use this sheet

quiz.why: The first principle of surveying is to work from the whole to the part, so errors do not accumulate.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Too-short tape makes measured length
quiz.why: A too-short tape needs more tape lengths to cover the same ground, so the measured length is longer than the true length.
A back bearing differs from the forward bearing by 180°. For 20°, add 180° to get 200°.

quiz.q: Mock 1: BS on BM 1.5, BM 10.0 ⇒ HI
quiz.why: HI = RL of the benchmark + backsight = 10.0 + 1.5 = 11.5.
Closely spaced contours mean a quick rise over a short horizontal distance, a steep slope.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Interior angle sum of pentagon
quiz.why: Interior angles sum to (2n − 4) × 90°. For a pentagon (n = 5), (10 − 4) × 90° = 540°.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Long chord for R 100, Δ 60°
Mock 1: GNSS accuracy class with base corrections
quiz.why: RTK GNSS uses base-station carrier-phase corrections to reach centimetre accuracy, while standalone GNSS gives metre-level accuracy.

questions.why: Plane surveying treats the earth's surface as flat over the area surveyed, so curvature is ignored.
The rise-and-fall check ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall involves intermediate sights, since every reading enters the rise or fall calculations.
Stadia instruments are made with multiplying constant k = f/i = 100.
S 30° E lies in the south-east quadrant, so WCB = 180° − 30° = 150°.

questions.q: True distance: 30 m tape 0.06 m too long, measured 450 m
questions.why: The tape's true length is 30.06 m, so true distance = 450 × 30.06/30 = 450.9 m. A tape that is too long gives readings that are too small, so the correction is added.
C_c = 0.0785d² = 0.0785 × 4 = 0.314 m, subtracted from readings (−0.314 m).
Departure = l sin θ = 120 sin 210° = 120 × (−0.5) = −60 m, i.e. westward.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Reciprocal levelling eliminates collimation error.  Reason (R): The error affects the two sets of readings in opposite senses, so averaging cancels it.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: the collimation error makes readings differ in opposite directions from the two instrument positions, so averaging the results cancels it. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Included angle: FB AB 60°, FB BC 160°
questions.why: BB of AB = 60° + 180° = 240°. Included angle = BB of AB − FB of BC = 240° − 160° = 80°.
The points form an 80 m by 50 m rectangle, with area 80 × 50 = 4000 m².

questions.q: Bowditch: ΣD = −0.24 m, perimeter 1200 m: correction to D of 400 m line
questions.why: The departures sum to −0.24, so the corrections must add +0.24. Bowditch correction = +0.24 × 400/1200 = +0.08 m.

questions.q: Case: A 1:2000 contour map has CI 1 m and contours 4 mm apart on the map. Ground slope
questions.why: At a scale of 1:2000, 4 mm on the map is 4 × 2000 = 8000 mm = 8 m on the ground. With a 1 m vertical interval the slope is 1 in 8.

questions.q: Reservoir trapezoidal volume: h 2 m, areas 1500, 2500, 3500 m²

Rankine total deflection after T₁ with sub-chord 8 m and one 20 m chord, R = 400
questions.why: The total deflection is the sum of deflections for the sub-chord and the chord: 1718.9 × (8 + 20)/400 = 1718.9 × 28/400 ≈ 120.3′.

questions.q: Total station: slope 500 m, zenith 87°: vertical difference
questions.why: Vertical difference = slope distance × cos(zenith angle) = 500 cos 87° ≈ 500 × 0.0523 = 26.17 m.

courses.title: Structural Analysis · Unit 1 · Determinacy, trusses, cables and arches
courses.summary: Static and kinematic indeterminacy of beams, frames and trusses, analysis of determinate plane trusses, cables under point and uniformly distributed loads, and three-hinged parabolic and circular arches (reactions, horizontal thrust, BM, normal thrust and radial shear).
outcomes: Find degrees of static and kinematic indeterminacy
Analyse determinate trusses quickly
Compute cable tensions and sag relations
Analyse three-hinged arches
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

story.title: Why some structures need more equations

scenes.text: A continuous bridge over three piers can't be solved by statics alone.
Its degree of indeterminacy tells how many compatibility equations are needed.

steps.title: Formulas (plane structures)
steps.body:
Static indeterminacy D_s:
- Beams/frames: D_s = (3m + r) − 3j − c (m members, r reactions, j joints, c releases) or D_s = r − 3 for simple beams (minus releases).
- Pin-jointed trusses: D_s = m + r − 2j.
Kinematic indeterminacy D_k (degrees of freedom): rigid frames D_k = 3j − r (minus constraints; neglecting axial deformation subtract members); trusses D_k = 2j − r.
D_s < 0 ⇒ unstable (mechanism); also check geometric instability.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Propped cantilever: r = 4 (fixed 3 + roller 1) ⇒ D_s = 1.

**Example 2.** Fixed beam: r = 6 ⇒ D_s = 3 (2 if axial forces ignored).

**Example 3.** Truss with m = 10, j = 6, r = 3: D_s = 10 + 3 − 12 = 1 (one redundant).

**Example 4.** Single-bay portal frame fixed at both bases: r = 6 ⇒ D_s = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting internal hinges (releases).
- Using truss formula for rigid frames.
- Calling a structure stable just because D_s ≥ 0 (check geometry).

activity.prompt: Truss: m = 13, j = 8, r = 3. Degree of static indeterminacy?

quiz.why: For a pin-jointed plane truss the static indeterminacy is D_s = m + r − 2j, with m members, r reactions and j joints.
A propped cantilever has 4 reactions (3 at the fixed end, 1 at the prop) against 3 equilibrium equations, so D_s = 1.
If D_s < 0, the structure has fewer restraints than needed for equilibrium, so it is an unstable mechanism.
A simply supported beam has 3 reactions (pin + roller) and 3 equations, so D_s = 0: statically determinate.
A beam fixed at both ends has 6 reactions in a plane and 3 equilibrium equations, so D_s = 6 − 3 = 3.

scenes.text: A factory roof uses Pratt and Howe trusses.
Knowing which members are in tension or compression guides member sizing.

steps.title: Methods recap
steps.body: Method of joints (two unknowns per joint), method of sections (cut ≤ 3 unknown members; moments about intersection points), zero-force member rules. For parallel-chord trusses under gravity loads: chords resist bending (top chord compression, bottom tension for simple span); diagonals resist shear (direction decides sign).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Pratt truss, 6 panels × 4 m, height 4 m, loads 10 kN at each bottom interior joint (5 loads): R = 25 kN. Bottom chord force in the central panel: M_centre = 25 × 12 − 10(8 + 4) = 180 kN·m ⇒ F = 180/4 = 45 kN (T).

**Example 2.** End diagonal (45°): vertical equilibrium at the end joint: F sin 45° = 25 ⇒ F = 35.4 kN.

**Example 3.** Howe vs Pratt: diagonals in Pratt are in tension (efficient for steel); in Howe they are in compression.

steps.title: Beam analogy
steps.body: Chord force ≈ M/h and diagonal vertical component ≈ V of an equivalent beam — a fast check.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the panel-point moment at the wrong section.
- Forgetting the angle when converting shear to diagonal force.
- Assuming all diagonals have the same sign in both truss types.

activity.prompt: Truss member → typical force (simple span, gravity load)

quiz.why: Taking moments about the opposite joint, chord force = beam bending moment/depth h, which is M/h (the internal couple).
The vertical component of a diagonal must carry the shear in that panel, so it equals the panel shear.
In a Pratt truss under gravity load the diagonals slope so that they are in tension, and the verticals carry compression.

quiz.q: R for symmetric truss with 5 loads of 10 kN
quiz.why: A symmetric truss carrying total 5 × 10 = 50 kN has each reaction equal to half: 25 kN.
The method of sections cuts the truss through no more than 3 members with unknown forces, as three equilibrium equations are available.

scenes.text: Suspension bridge cables carry the deck by pure tension.
Under a uniform horizontal load, a cable takes a parabolic shape.

steps.title: Cable relations
steps.body:
Cable supports at the same level, span L, sag d, UDL w per horizontal length:
H = wL²/(8d); V = wL/2 at each support; T_max = √(H² + V²) = (wL/2)√(1 + L²/(16d²)).
Shape y = 4dx(L − x)/L² (parabola). General cable theorem: H × (cable sag at a point) = BM of an equivalent simply supported beam at that point.
Length ≈ L + 8d²/(3L).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L = 100 m, d = 10 m, w = 20 kN/m: H = 20 × 10 000/80 = 2500 kN; V = 1000 kN; T_max = 2693 kN.

**Example 2.** Cable length ≈ 100 + 8 × 100/300 = 102.67 m.

**Example 3.** Point loads: cable 30 m span with 10 kN at third points and sag 3 m at the loads: equivalent beam BM at the load = 10 × 10 = 100 kN·m ⇒ H = 33.3 kN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total load instead of load per unit length in H.
- Forgetting the horizontal component H is constant along the cable.
- Using the catenary vs parabola interchangeably for large sags (parabola assumes load per horizontal length).

activity.prompt: Cable: span 60 m, sag 6 m, w = 10 kN/m. Horizontal tension H (kN)?

quiz.q: Horizontal tension of a parabolic cable
quiz.why: For a cable with UDL, taking moments of the half span about the lowest point gives H d = wL²/8, so H = wL²/(8d).

quiz.q: H along a cable under vertical loads is
quiz.why: Under vertical loads there are no horizontal forces, so the horizontal component H is the same at every point along the cable.
T = √(H² + V²) with H constant, so tension is maximum where the vertical component is greatest, at the supports.
Under a UDL per horizontal length, the cable shape is a parabola (a catenary arises under its own weight).
H = wL²/(8d), so a larger sag d gives a smaller horizontal tension.

scenes.text: Old stone bridges are arches carrying load mostly in compression.
A three-hinged arch is statically determinate — the crown hinge gives the extra equation.

steps.title: Analysis
steps.body:
Reactions: V_A, V_B from moments as for a beam; horizontal thrust H from M = 0 at the crown hinge.
Parabolic arch (span L, rise h, UDL w over full span): H = wL²/(8h), BM = 0 everywhere — pure compression (funicular).
BM at a section: M = M_beam − H y (y = arch ordinate). Normal thrust N = V sin θ + H cos θ; radial shear Q = V cos θ − H sin θ (θ = slope of arch axis).
Parabola y = 4hx(L − x)/L²; slope tan θ = 4h(L − 2x)/L².

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Parabolic arch L = 40 m, h = 8 m, point load 100 kN at 10 m from A: V_A = 75, V_B = 25 kN. Crown (x = 20): M = 0 ⇒ 25 × 20 − H × 8 = 0 ⇒ H = 62.5 kN.
At x = 10: y = 4 × 8 × 10 × 30/1600 = 6 m; M = 75 × 10 − 62.5 × 6 = 375 kN·m.

**Example 2.** Same arch with UDL 10 kN/m full span: H = 10 × 1600/64 = 250 kN; BM = 0 everywhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the beam BM without subtracting H y.
- Taking moments at the crown using both sides' loads.

For a parabolic three-hinged arch under full UDL, the arch axis coincides with the thrust line, so the bending moment is zero everywhere and only axial compression exists.
The bending moment at any section of an arch is the beam moment minus the thrust moment: M = M_beam − H y. The horizontal thrust reduces the bending.
A three-hinged arch has 4 reactions and 3 equilibrium equations plus 1 equation from the hinge condition at the crown, so it is statically determinate.

A flexible cable has no bending stiffness, so it can resist only tension.
An arch's horizontal thrust produces a moment −Hy that offsets the beam moment, which reduces bending.

options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

BM at x = 5 m for the arch above (y = 3.75 m)

outcomes: Apply the moment-area theorems and conjugate beam
