scenes.text: A site engineer quickly checks a cantilever's tip deflection without integrating.
Moment-area uses the area of the M/EI diagram.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
**Theorem I:** change in slope between A and B = area of M/EI diagram between them.
**Theorem II:** deviation of B from the tangent at A = first moment (about B) of the M/EI area between A and B.
Use a reference tangent where slope is known (fixed support; mid-span of symmetric beams). Parabolic areas: complete parabola under UDL — area 2/3 bh, centroid at mid; spandrel (cantilever UDL BM) area 1/3 bh, centroid 1/4 from the vertex... (3/4 from the base side).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cantilever end load W: M/EI triangle area = WL²/(2EI) ⇒ slope at tip WL²/2EI; centroid 2L/3 from the tip ⇒ deflection = WL²/2EI × 2L/3 = WL³/3EI ✔.

**Example 2.** Simply supported central load W: from mid-span (horizontal tangent), area of half M/EI = ½ × L/2 × WL/(4EI) = WL²/(16EI) = slope at support; deflection = WL²/16EI × (2/3)(L/2) = WL³/48EI ✔.

**Example 3.** Cantilever UDL: area = wL³/(6EI) ⇒ tip slope; centroid 3L/4 from the tip ⇒ δ = wL⁴/(8EI) ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking moments of the area about the wrong point (must be about the point whose deviation is sought).
- Using a reference tangent with unknown slope.
- Spandrel centroid location errors.

activity.prompt: Cantilever, end load 10 kN, L = 3 m, EI = 9000 kN·m². Tip slope WL²/(2EI) in radians?

quiz.why: Moment-area Theorem I states that the change in slope between two points equals the area of the M/EI diagram between them.
Theorem II gives the tangential deviation of one point from the tangent at another: the moment of the M/EI area about that point.

quiz.q: Reference tangent for symmetric SS beam
quiz.why: For a symmetric simply supported beam under symmetric load the slope at mid-span is zero, so the tangent there is horizontal and a convenient reference.
The M/EI diagram of a cantilever with UDL is a parabola of height wL²/2EI. Its area is (1/3) × L × wL²/2EI = wL³/(6EI).

quiz.q: Cantilever tip deflection from area × centroid
quiz.why: By Theorem II, deflection = area of M/EI × distance of centroid = (1/2)(WL/EI)(L) × (2L/3) = WL³/(3EI).

scenes.text: Instead of integrating, load an imaginary beam with M/EI.
Its shear gives the slope and its moment gives the deflection of the real beam.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
Load the conjugate beam with M/EI diagram (sagging M → downward load or as per convention). Slope of real beam = shear in conjugate beam; deflection = BM in conjugate beam.
Support conversions: fixed ↔ free; free ↔ fixed; simple end ↔ simple end; interior support ↔ internal hinge; internal hinge ↔ interior support.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Simply supported, UDL: conjugate beam simply supported with parabolic load of peak wL²/(8EI); total = (2/3)L × wL²/(8EI) = wL³/(12EI); reaction = wL³/(24EI) = end slope ✔; mid BM = wL³/24EI × L/2 − (wL³/24EI)(3L/16) = 5wL⁴/(384EI) ✔.

**Example 2.** Cantilever: conjugate is fixed at the (real) free end — the BM at that fixed end gives the tip deflection WL³/3EI ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong support conversion (fixed must become free).
- Sign convention of the M/EI loading.
- Using real-beam reactions on the conjugate beam.

activity.prompt: Real support → conjugate support

quiz.q: Slope of real beam equals conjugate beam's
quiz.why: In the conjugate beam method the slope of the real beam equals the shear force in the conjugate beam.

quiz.q: Deflection of real beam equals conjugate beam's
quiz.why: The deflection of the real beam equals the bending moment in the conjugate beam, loaded with M/EI.
A fixed end (zero slope and deflection) of the real beam becomes a free end in the conjugate beam, which has no shear or moment.

quiz.q: End slope of SS beam with UDL
quiz.why: The end slope of a simply supported beam with UDL is wL³/(24EI), equal to the end reaction of the conjugate beam.
The conjugate beam is loaded with the M/EI diagram of the real beam.

scenes.text: A roof truss's mid-span joint must not sag more than span/325.
Apply a virtual unit load at that joint and sum member contributions.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Beams/frames: δ = ∫ M m dx/(EI) (M real moment, m moment due to unit load at the point in the desired direction); slope: unit couple.
Trusses: δ = Σ P u L/(AE) (P real member force, u member force due to unit load).
Temperature/fabrication errors in trusses: δ = Σ u (αΔT L) or Σ u ΔL.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cantilever end load W: M = −Wx, m = −x ⇒ δ = ∫₀ᴸ Wx²dx/EI = WL³/3EI ✔.

**Example 2.** Truss (3 members) with table: members AB: P = 20, u = 0.5, L = 4, AE = 10⁵; BC: −28.3, −0.707, 2.83; AC: −28.3, −0.707, 2.83 (kN, m): Σ PuL = 40 + 56.6 + 56.6 = 153.2 ⇒ δ = 153.2/10⁵ = 1.53 mm (all AE equal).

**Example 3.** A member 2 mm too long with u = 0.6 ⇒ joint displacement contribution 1.2 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inconsistent sign conventions between P and u.
- Units (kN, m, kN/m² for AE → m).
- Applying the unit load in the wrong direction (answer sign shows direction).

activity.prompt: Unit-load method for a truss joint deflection
items: Find real member forces P under the actual loads
Remove real loads; apply a unit load at the joint in the desired direction
Find member forces u due to the unit load
Tabulate PuL/AE for each member
Sum the column to get the deflection (sign gives direction)

quiz.why: By the unit-load (virtual work) method for trusses, deflection = Σ P u L/(AE), where P is the actual force and u the force due to the unit load.

quiz.q: For slope by unit-load method apply
quiz.why: To find a rotation by the unit-load method, apply a unit couple at that point, as the work is done by the rotation.
For beams, virtual work gives δ = ∫ M m dx/EI, where m is the moment due to the unit load.
A negative answer means the deflection is in the direction opposite to the assumed direction of the unit load.
options: deflection opposite to the unit load direction

quiz.why: For temperature change in a truss, the deflection is Σ u α ΔT L, with u from the unit load.

lessons.title: Strain energy, Castigliano and reciprocal theorems

scenes.text: Structures store energy as they deform — like springs.
Differentiate the energy with respect to a load to get the deflection under it.

steps.title: Theorems
steps.body:
Strain energy: axial U = ΣP²L/(2AE); bending U = ∫M²dx/(2EI); torsion ∫T²dx/(2GJ).
**Castigliano I (for deflection):** δᵢ = ∂U/∂Pᵢ (linear elastic). For rotation use ∂U/∂Mᵢ; for a point with no load apply a fictitious load and set it to zero after differentiating.
**Castigliano II / least work:** for redundant R, ∂U/∂R = 0 (compatibility).
**Maxwell–Betti:** δ_ij = δ_ji (deflection at i due to unit load at j equals deflection at j due to unit load at i); P₁δ₁₂ = P₂δ₂₁ (Betti).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Cantilever end load: U = ∫W²x²dx/(2EI) = W²L³/(6EI) ⇒ δ = ∂U/∂W = WL³/(3EI) ✔.

**Example 2.** Propped cantilever with UDL by least work: U = ∫(Rx − wx²/2)²dx/(2EI); ∂U/∂R = 0 ⇒ RL³/3 − wL⁴/8 = 0 ⇒ R = 3wL/8 ✔.

**Example 3.** Maxwell: a 10 kN load at C deflects D by 2 mm ⇒ a 10 kN load at D deflects C by 2 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Castigliano to non-linear systems.
- Forgetting to set the fictitious load to zero.
- Using Maxwell's theorem for non-linear or non-elastic behaviour.

activity.prompt: Propped cantilever (span 8 m) with UDL 6 kN/m: prop reaction 3wL/8 (kN)?

quiz.why: Castigliano's theorem says that the partial derivative of the strain energy with respect to a load equals the deflection under that load: δ = ∂U/∂P.

quiz.q: Least work principle for redundant R
quiz.why: The principle of least work says that for a redundant reaction R, the strain energy is a minimum with respect to it, ∂U/∂R = 0 (when the support does not move).
Maxwell's reciprocal theorem: the deflection at i due to a unit load at j equals the deflection at j due to a unit load at i, δ_ij = δ_ji.
Strain energy due to bending is U = ∫M²dx/(2EI).

quiz.q: Prop reaction for propped cantilever with UDL
quiz.why: Using least work, the prop reaction for a propped cantilever with UDL is R = 3wL/8.

questions.why: The conjugate of a free end is a fixed end, and vice versa.
The unit-load method is based on the principle of virtual work.
Maxwell's theorem relies on linear elastic behaviour, since it uses superposition and the symmetry of the flexibility matrix.
The slope at the tip of a cantilever with UDL is the area of the M/EI diagram: wL³/(6EI).

questions.q: Truss member: P 30 kN, u 0.8, L 5 m, AE 2×10⁵ kN: contribution
End slope of SS beam with central load W
questions.why: The slope at the end of a simply supported beam with central load W is WL²/(16EI).

questions.q: Assertion (A): Strain energy method gives deflection under a load directly via ∂U/∂P.  Reason (R): For linear elastic structures U is a quadratic function of loads.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: for a linear elastic structure U is quadratic in the loads, so its derivative ∂U/∂P gives the displacement corresponding to P (Castigliano), explaining the assertion.

questions.q: Cantilever 4 m, end load 15 kN, EI 20 000 kN·m²: δ
SS 6 m, UDL 10 kN/m, EI 50 000 kN·m²: mid deflection
Propped cantilever UDL: fixed-end moment magnitude
questions.why: The fixed-end moment of a propped cantilever with UDL is M = wL²/2 − R_prop L = wL²/2 − (3wL/8)L = wL²/8.

questions.q: Case: A truss joint deflection table gives Σ PuL = 240 kN·m (AE = 1.2×10⁵ kN for all members). Deflection
Strain energy of a bar: P 100 kN, L 2 m, AE 4×10⁵ kN
Cantilever with load W at mid-length: tip deflection
questions.why: Deflection at mid-length of a cantilever is W(L/2)³/(3EI) = WL³/24EI, and the slope there is W(L/2)²/(2EI) = WL²/8EI. The tip extends straight: δ = WL³/24EI + WL²/8EI × L/2 = WL³/24EI + WL³/16EI = 5WL³/(48EI).

questions.q: A 20 kN load at point 1 causes 4 mm deflection at point 2. A 40 kN load at point 2 causes at point 1
questions.why: By Maxwell's reciprocal theorem, the flexibility f₂₁ = f₁₂ = 4 mm/20 kN = 0.2 mm/kN. So a 40 kN load at point 2 causes 40 × 0.2 = 8 mm at point 1.

questions.q: Fictitious load in Castigliano is set to
questions.why: A fictitious load is introduced to find the deflection at a point with no real load, and it is set to zero after the differentiation.

courses.title: Structural Analysis · Unit 3 · Influence lines and moving loads
courses.summary: Concept of influence lines, ILD for reactions, shear and bending moment in simply supported and overhanging beams, Müller-Breslau principle, maximum SF and BM due to a point load, UDL longer/shorter than span and a train of wheel loads, absolute maximum bending moment, and ILD for truss members.
outcomes: Draw ILDs for reactions, SF and BM
Use Müller-Breslau to sketch ILDs
Find maximum effects of point loads, UDLs and wheel trains
Find the absolute maximum BM in a simply supported girder
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: As a truck rolls across a bridge, forces at each section change.
An influence line shows the effect of a unit load at every position.

steps.title: Simply supported beam (span L)
steps.body:
- ILD R_A: straight line from 1 at A to 0 at B.
- ILD shear at section C (distance a from A, b from B): from 0 at A to −a/L just left of C; jump to +b/L just right of C; then to 0 at B.
- ILD BM at C: triangle with peak ab/L at C.
Effect of a point load W at a position = W × ordinate; of a UDL w = w × area of the ILD under it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L = 10 m, section C at 4 m: BM ILD peak = 4 × 6/10 = 2.4 m. Load 50 kN at C ⇒ M = 120 kN·m.

**Example 2.** UDL 10 kN/m over the whole span: M_C = 10 × area = 10 × ½ × 10 × 2.4 = 120 kN·m.

**Example 3.** Shear at C: max positive due to UDL placed from C to B: area = ½ × 6 × 0.6 = 1.8 ⇒ 18 kN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing ILD with BMD (ILD is for a fixed section and moving load).
- Forgetting the sign change across the section in shear ILD.
- Using ordinate instead of area for UDLs.

activity.prompt: SS beam 12 m: ILD BM ordinate at a section 3 m from A (m)?

quiz.why: An influence line diagram shows how a particular effect (reaction, shear or moment) at one fixed section varies as a unit load moves across the structure.
options: effect at a fixed section of a moving unit load

quiz.q: ILD for R_A of SS beam
quiz.why: For a simply supported beam, R_A = 1 when the unit load is at A, and falls linearly to 0 at B, so the ILD is a triangle.
options: triangle: 1 at A to 0 at B

quiz.q: Peak of BM ILD at C
quiz.why: The BM influence line at section C is a triangle with peak ordinate ab/L, where a and b are the distances of C from A and B.
The effect of a UDL on a section is w times the area of the ILD under the loaded length.

quiz.q: Shear ILD jumps at the section by
quiz.why: The shear influence line at a section has a sudden jump of 1 where the unit load crosses it.

scenes.text: Remove the restraint for the quantity you want and give it a unit displacement.
The deflected shape is the influence line.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
The ILD of a force/moment equals the deflected shape when the corresponding restraint is removed and a unit displacement (or rotation) is applied in its direction.
- Reaction: remove support, push up by 1.
- Shear at C: cut with a 'slider' (relative vertical displacement 1, slopes parallel).
- Moment at C: insert a hinge, apply unit relative rotation.
For determinate structures ILDs are straight lines; for indeterminate ones they are curves.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Overhanging beam (supports A and B, overhang to D): ILD for R_B extends beyond B with ordinate > 1 at the overhang end (= (L + c)/L).

**Example 2.** BM at mid-span of a continuous beam: curved ILD with negative ordinates in adjacent spans ⇒ load alternate spans for maximum.

**Example 3.** Shear ILD of a cantilever at a section: 1 for loads beyond the section toward the free end, 0 elsewhere.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving a rotation instead of a displacement for force ILDs.
- Forgetting ordinates beyond overhangs.
- Drawing straight ILDs for indeterminate structures.

statements.s: ILDs of determinate structures consist of straight lines.
ILD for BM is found by inserting a hinge and applying a unit rotation.
ILDs of continuous beams are straight lines.
Overhang ILD ordinate for R_B can exceed 1.

quiz.why: The Müller-Breslau principle says the ILD for an effect has the shape of the deflected shape of the structure when that restraint is removed and a unit displacement given there.

quiz.q: For shear ILD the release is
quiz.why: For a shear ILD the restraint released is the shear resistance, by inserting a sliding (shear) release, while keeping bending moment and axial force.

quiz.q: Simply supported span AB = 10 m with a 2 m overhang beyond support B. ILD ordinate for R_B at the overhang tip:
quiz.why: With a unit load at distance x from A, R_B = x/L, a straight line that carries on into the overhang. At the tip x = 10 + 2 = 12 m, so the ordinate is 12/10 = 1.2.

quiz.q: Maximum mid-span moment in continuous beams: load
quiz.why: For the maximum positive mid-span moment in a continuous beam, load the span itself and alternate spans, since those parts of the ILD are positive.
ILDs for statically indeterminate structures are curved because they follow the elastic deflected shape, which is not made of straight lines.

scenes.text: A bridge must be safe for the worst position of every vehicle.
Simple rules place loads to maximise each effect.

steps.title: Rules (SS beam, section C)
steps.body:
- **Single point load W:** max BM at C when W is at C: Wab/L. Max +SF: just right of C: Wb/L; max −SF: just left: Wa/L.
- **UDL longer than span:** max BM at C: cover the whole span: w ab/2; max +SF: load from C to B.
- **UDL shorter than span (length d):** max BM at C when C divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span.
- **Train of wheel loads:** max BM at C when the average load on AC equals the average on CB (a load is at C).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** L = 20 m, C at 5 m, W = 100 kN: max BM at C = 100 × 5 × 15/20 = 375 kN·m.

**Example 2.** UDL 4 m long (w = 30 kN/m) on 20 m span, C at 5 m: position so that C divides it 1:3 ⇒ 1 m to the left of C, 3 m to the right. Ordinates: peak 3.75; at 4 m from A: 3.0; at 8 m: 3.0 ⇒ area = ½(3.0 + 3.75)×1 + ½(3.75 + 3.0)×3 = 3.375 + 10.125 = 13.5 ⇒ M = 405 kN·m.

**Example 3.** Max reaction R_A for a 2-wheel load (60 kN, 40 kN, 2 m apart) on 10 m span: place 60 kN at A: R_A = 60 + 40 × 0.8 = 92 kN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the UDL centred on C regardless of the section position.
- Forgetting to try each wheel at the section for wheel trains.
- Missing negative shear maxima.

activity.prompt: SS 16 m, section at 4 m, single moving load 80 kN. Maximum BM at the section (kN·m)?

quiz.q: Max BM at C from a point load occurs with the load
quiz.why: The BM at C from a single moving point load is greatest when the load is at C, where the ILD ordinate is the peak.

quiz.q: Max +SF at C (point load) occurs with load
quiz.why: The shear ILD at C has a positive part to the right of C, so the max positive shear occurs with the load just to the right of C.

quiz.q: UDL shorter than span: max BM at C when
quiz.why: For a UDL shorter than the span, BM at C is maximum when C divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span.
options: C divides the load as it divides the span

quiz.q: Wheel train rule for BM at C
quiz.why: For a train of wheel loads, maximum BM at C occurs when the average load on the left of C equals the average load on the right.
options: average load left = average load right

quiz.q: UDL longer than span: max BM at C
quiz.why: A UDL covering the full span gives max BM at C equal to w × area of the ILD = w × ½ × L × (ab/L) = w ab/2.

lessons.title: Absolute maximum bending moment and truss ILDs

scenes.text: An overhead crane runs on girders; wheel loads move along them.
The absolute maximum moment occurs near — but not exactly at — mid-span.

steps.title: Absolute maximum BM (wheel train on SS girder)
steps.body:
Place the loads so that the centre-line of the span bisects the distance between the resultant R of the loads on the span and the nearest heavy wheel; the absolute max BM occurs under that wheel.
For two equal loads W at spacing x: max under one load when the span centre is midway between that load and the resultant: M_abs = (W/(2L))(L − x/2)²·... (for two equal loads: M = W(L − x/2)²/(2L)).

steps.title: ILD for truss members
steps.body: Use method of sections with a unit load at panel points: chord forces ∝ ILD of BM at the opposite panel point divided by height; diagonal forces ∝ ILD of panel shear divided by sin θ. Loads transfer through stringers and cross-girders to panel points, so ILDs are straight between panel points.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two 100 kN loads 4 m apart on a 20 m span: resultant at the middle of the pair; place span centre 1 m from one load ⇒ loads at 9 m and 13 m from A... (load under consideration at 9 m): R_A = 200 × (20 − 11)/20 = 90 kN; M = 90 × 9 = 810 kN·m. Formula: 100 × (20 − 2)²/(2 × 20) = 810 ✔.

**Example 2.** If both loads were at mid-span symmetrically (8 and 12 m): M at 8 m = 100 × 8 = 800 kN·m (< 810).

**Example 3.** Pratt truss bottom chord ILD = (BM ILD at the top panel point)/h — triangle with peak ab/(Lh).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming absolute max is at mid-span.
- Forgetting to check under each heavy wheel.
- Treating truss ILDs as continuous curves between panel points.

activity.prompt: Finding absolute maximum BM for a wheel train
items: Find the resultant of the loads on the span and its position
Pick a heavy wheel near the resultant
Place the loads so the span centre bisects the distance between the resultant and that wheel
Compute reactions and the BM under that wheel
Repeat for other wheels and take the largest

quiz.why: The absolute maximum BM in a simply supported beam under moving loads occurs under a wheel close to mid-span, when mid-span bisects the distance between that wheel and the resultant.

quiz.q: Two equal loads W at spacing x on span L: M_abs
quiz.why: For two equal loads W at spacing x, the resultant is midway, and placing the mid-span midway between a wheel and the resultant gives M_max = W(L − x/2)²/(2L).
The ILD for a truss chord force is the BM ILD at the panel point opposite the member, divided by the lever arm h.
options: BM ILD at opposite panel point / h

quiz.q: Truss ILDs between panel points are
quiz.why: In a truss, loads are transferred through the floor system to panel points, so ILDs are straight lines between panel points.
The vertical component of a diagonal carries the panel shear, so the diagonal's force ILD is the panel shear ILD divided by sin θ.

questions.q: ILD ordinate for R_A at mid-span (SS)
questions.why: R_A falls linearly from 1 at A to 0 at B, so at mid-span the ordinate is 0.5.
The Müller-Breslau principle uses a unit displacement at the released restraint, and the deflected shape gives the influence line.
options: unit displacement at the released restraint

questions.q: Maximum BM at a section from a point load: load at
questions.why: The max BM at a given section from a single point load occurs when the load is at that section, where the ILD ordinate is largest.

questions.q: BM ILD peak for C at 2 m on 8 m span
Max BM at that section from 60 kN
questions.why: Max BM = load × peak ordinate = 60 × 1.5 = 90 kN·m.

questions.q: UDL 20 kN/m longer than span 8 m: max BM at that section
questions.why: A UDL covering the whole span gives M = w × ILD area = 20 × (½ × 8 × 1.5) = 20 × 6 = 120 kN·m. (Equal to w ab/2 = 20 × 2 × 6/2.)

questions.q: Assertion (A): ILDs for determinate beams are made of straight lines.  Reason (R): Releasing one restraint makes the beam a mechanism that moves as rigid bodies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: releasing one restraint of a determinate beam turns it into a mechanism that moves as rigid bodies, so the deflected shape is made of straight lines, and the reason explains the straight-line ILDs.

questions.q: Max +SF at 3 m section of 12 m span due to 40 kN
questions.why: The positive shear ILD to the right of the section has a maximum ordinate b/L = 9/12 = 0.75, so SF = 40 × 0.75 = 30 kN.

questions.q: Max −SF at that section due to 40 kN
questions.why: The negative ordinate just left of the section is a/L = 3/12 = 0.25, so max negative SF = 40 × 0.25 = 10 kN.

questions.q: Two 50 kN wheels 2 m apart on 10 m span: absolute max BM
questions.why: Resultant 100 kN is midway. Place the mid-span halfway between the resultant and the nearer wheel. R_A = 100 × 4.5/10 = 45 kN. M under the wheel at 4.5 m = 45 × 4.5 = 202.5 kN·m, i.e. W(L − x/2)²/(2L) with W = 50.

questions.q: Case: A 30 m bridge, section 10 m from A, a 6 m UDL of 40 kN/m. For max BM at the section, the UDL should extend from
questions.why: Max BM occurs when the section divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span: 10 m : 20 m = 1:2. Of the 6 m load, 2 m lies left of the section and 4 m right, so it covers 8 m to 14 m.

questions.q: ILD for R_B at overhang end (span 8 m, overhang 2 m)
questions.why: With a unit load at distance x from A and the overhang beyond B, R_B = x/L. At the overhang end x = 8 + 2 = 10 m, so the ordinate is 10/8 = 1.25.

questions.q: Max BM in that case (peak ab/L = 10·20/30 = 6.67; ordinates at 8 m and 14 m: 5.33 each)
Bottom chord ILD peak for panel point at 6 m on 18 m truss, h = 3 m
Max R_A for wheels 80 kN and 40 kN 3 m apart on 12 m span
questions.why: Place the 80 kN wheel at A and the 40 kN wheel 3 m away. R_A = 80 + 40 × (12 − 3)/12 = 80 + 30 = 110 kN.

courses.title: Structural Analysis · Unit 4 · Indeterminate structures: consistent deformation, slope-deflection, moment distribution
courses.summary: Fixed-end moments, propped cantilevers and fixed beams by consistent deformations, slope-deflection equations for continuous beams and frames (with and without sway), moment distribution (stiffness, carry-over, distribution factors), and an introduction to the stiffness matrix method.
outcomes: Analyse propped cantilevers and fixed beams
Apply slope-deflection equations to continuous beams
Use moment distribution with distribution and carry-over factors
Outline the matrix stiffness method
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A beam built into walls at both ends deflects far less than a simply supported one.
End fixity creates hogging moments that reduce the mid-span sagging moment.

steps.title: Fixed-end moments (FEM, clockwise positive at the left end... magnitudes)
steps.body:
- Central point load W: WL/8 at each end (hogging); mid-span +WL/8; δ = WL³/(192EI).
- Point load at a (b from B): M_A = Wab²/L², M_B = Wa²b/L².
- UDL: wL²/12 at each end; mid +wL²/24; δ = wL⁴/(384EI).
- Sinking of support Δ: 6EIΔ/L² at each end.
Propped cantilever (UDL): R_prop = 3wL/8; M_fixed = wL²/8; max sagging 9wL²/128 at 3L/8 from the prop.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Fixed beam 6 m, UDL 20 kN/m: FEM = 60 kN·m; mid-span = 30 kN·m.

**Example 2.** Fixed beam 8 m, 40 kN at 2 m from A: M_A = 40 × 2 × 36/64 = 45, M_B = 40 × 4 × 6/64 = 15 kN·m.

**Example 3.** Propped cantilever 4 m, central load W: by consistent deformation δ_W − δ_R = 0 ⇒ R = 5W/16.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping a and b in Wab²/L².
- Forgetting signs (hogging at supports).
- Using SS formulas for fixed beams.

activity.prompt: Fixed beam 5 m with UDL 24 kN/m. Fixed-end moment magnitude (kN·m)?

quiz.why: For a fixed beam with a central point load W, the fixed-end moment is WL/8.
For a fixed beam with a UDL, the fixed-end moment is wL²/12.

quiz.q: Prop reaction for central load W (propped cantilever)
quiz.why: By consistent deformation, a propped cantilever with a central point load has a prop reaction of 5W/16.
For a fixed beam with UDL, the mid-span moment is wL²/8 − wL²/12 = wL²/24 (sagging).

quiz.q: FEM due to support sinking Δ
quiz.why: When one end of a fixed beam settles by Δ relative to the other, the fixed-end moment is 6EIΔ/L².

scenes.text: Floor beams run continuously over several columns.
Slope-deflection writes each end moment in terms of joint rotations.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
M_AB = FEM_AB + (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3ψ), M_BA = FEM_BA + (2EI/L)(2θ_B + θ_A − 3ψ), ψ = Δ/L (chord rotation). Clockwise moments positive (on the member ends).
Joint equilibrium: ΣM at each free joint = 0. Far end pinned: use modified M_AB = FEM′ + (3EI/L)θ_A.
Sway frames: add a shear (storey) equation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two-span continuous beam ABC, A and C fixed, B a simple support, spans 4 m, UDL 12 kN/m on both, EI constant. FEM = ∓16 kN·m. By symmetry θ_B = 0 ⇒ M_BA = +16, M_BC = −16 (balanced).

**Example 2.** Same but load only on AB: M_BA = 16 + (2EI/4)(2θ_B), M_BC = (2EI/4)(2θ_B). ΣM_B = 0 ⇒ 16 + 2EIθ_B = 0 ⇒ EIθ_B = −8 ⇒ M_BA = 8, M_BC = −8, M_AB = −16 + 0.5EIθ_B = −20 kN·m, M_CB = −4 kN·m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign convention mix-ups (use clockwise-positive consistently).
- Forgetting chord rotation when supports settle or frames sway.
- Using 2EI/L for a pinned far end (use the modified 3EI/L form).

activity.prompt: Slope-deflection
activity.text: M_AB = FEM_AB + (2EI/L)(2θ_A + θ_B − 3ψ). With far end pinned the stiffness term becomes ___EI/L × θ_A, and the carry-over factor to a fixed far end is ___.

quiz.why: The slope-deflection method is a displacement method, so its unknowns are joint rotations and sway displacements, not forces.
The chord rotation due to relative displacement Δ of the ends is ψ = Δ/L.
At each joint, the sum of the end moments of the members meeting there is zero. This is the equilibrium equation for the unknown joint rotation.

quiz.q: Stiffness of member with far end fixed
quiz.why: The rotational stiffness of a member with the far end fixed is 4EI/L, the moment for a unit rotation at the near end.
This refers to the worked example in the lesson, whose solution gives M_AB = −20 kN·m (hogging at A).

scenes.text: Before computers, engineers designed tall buildings with Hardy Cross's moment distribution.
Lock joints, then release and balance them iteratively.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
Stiffness k = 4EI/L (far end fixed) or 3EI/L (far end pinned, then carry-over 0). Distribution factor DF = k/Σk at a joint. Carry-over factor = ½ to a fixed far end.
Steps: compute FEMs; at each joint distribute unbalanced moment (−sum × DF); carry over half to far ends; repeat until small. Fixed supports DF = 0; pinned end DF = 1.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Beam ABC: A fixed, B continuous support, C fixed; AB = 6 m (UDL 10 kN/m), BC = 4 m (no load), EI constant.
k_BA = 4EI/6 = 0.667EI, k_BC = 4EI/4 = EI ⇒ DF_BA = 0.4, DF_BC = 0.6.
FEM_AB = −30, FEM_BA = +30. Unbalanced at B = +30 ⇒ distribute −12 (BA), −18 (BC). Carry over −6 to A, −9 to C.
Final: M_AB = −36, M_BA = 18, M_BC = −18, M_CB = −9 kN·m (one cycle suffices here).

**Example 2.** If C were pinned: k_BC = 3EI/4 = 0.75EI ⇒ DF_BA = 0.471, DF_BC = 0.529.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Carrying over to a pinned end.
- Using DF ≠ 0 at fixed supports.
- Wrong sign when distributing (distribute the negative of the unbalance).

activity.prompt: Joint with k₁ = 2EI and k₂ = 3EI. Distribution factor of member 1?

quiz.why: The distribution factor of a member at a joint is its stiffness divided by the total stiffness of the members there, k/Σk.
For a prismatic member with the far end fixed, half of the moment applied at one end is carried over to the other: carry-over factor 1/2.
If the far end is pinned (or a roller), the stiffness is reduced to 3EI/L.
A fixed support cannot rotate, so it takes the full moment and does not distribute: DF = 0 in the sense of no rotation-based distribution.
Moment distribution (Hardy Cross) is an iterative relaxation method: balance joints and carry over, repeating until the unbalanced moments are negligible.

lessons.title: Sway frames and the stiffness matrix method

scenes.text: Wind pushes a portal frame sideways.
Modern software uses the stiffness matrix method — the same ideas, organised as matrices.

steps.title: Sway in frames
steps.body: Unsymmetric loading or geometry causes sway Δ. Approach: (i) non-sway analysis with a temporary prop; (ii) arbitrary sway moments 6EIΔ/L²; (iii) superpose to satisfy the storey shear equation (sum of column shears = applied horizontal load).

steps.title: Stiffness matrix method
steps.body: Member stiffness (beam element, ignoring axial): [[12EI/L³, 6EI/L², −12EI/L³, 6EI/L²], [6EI/L², 4EI/L, −6EI/L², 2EI/L], …]. Assemble global K, apply boundary conditions, solve K D = F for displacements, then member forces. Flexibility method is the force-based dual. Basis of FEM software (STAAD, ETABS, etc. — used nominatively).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Portal frame, fixed bases, columns h = 4 m, horizontal load 20 kN at top, rigid beam (EI_beam ≫): each column shear 10 kN ⇒ end moments 10 × 4/2 = 20 kN·m (double curvature).

**Example 2.** Same frame with pinned bases: each column shear 10 kN, moment at top 40 kN·m, zero at base.

**Example 3.** Rotational stiffness term 4EI/L for L = 5 m, EI = 10⁴ kN·m² = 8000 kN·m/rad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the sway equation.
- Assuming the beam is rigid when it isn't (approximation only).
- Mixing local and global coordinates in the stiffness method.

activity.prompt: Concept → description
pairs: Solve K D = F for displacements

quiz.why: Sway occurs in frames with unsymmetrical loading or geometry (or lateral loads), because the joints then move sideways.
The stiffness (displacement) method takes joint displacements as the unknowns, solves for them, and then finds member forces.

quiz.q: Fixed-end moment due to sway Δ (both ends fixed)
quiz.why: The fixed-end moment due to a relative sway Δ between the ends of a fixed member is 6EIΔ/L².

quiz.q: Column moment for fixed-base rigid-beam portal (V per column 15 kN, h 4 m)
quiz.why: Each column of a fixed-base portal with a rigid beam has inflexion at mid-height, so the base moment is V × h/2 = 15 × 4/2 = 30 kN·m.

quiz.q: Element stiffness term for rotation at near end
quiz.why: In the element stiffness matrix, the term for rotation at the near end due to unit rotation there is 4EI/L.

questions.q: FEM for UDL on fixed beam
questions.why: The fixed-end moment for a UDL on a fixed beam is wL²/12.
The carry-over factor for a prismatic member with far end fixed is 0.5.
Slope-deflection takes joint rotations and sway as unknowns, so it is a displacement (stiffness) method.

questions.q: FEM for point load 30 kN at 2 m on 6 m fixed beam: M_A
questions.why: M_A = W a b²/L² = 30 × 2 × 4²/6² = 30 × 2 × 16/36 ≈ 26.7 kN·m (the nearer end has the larger moment).

questions.q: Distribution factors at a joint for members of stiffness 4EI/4 and 4EI/2 (far ends fixed)
questions.why: Stiffness 4EI/4 = EI and 4EI/2 = 2EI, in ratio 1:2. DF = k/Σk gives 1/3 and 2/3.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Moment distribution converges because distribution and carry-over factors are less than one.  Reason (R): Each cycle reduces the unbalanced moments geometrically.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: each cycle multiplies the unbalanced moment by factors less than one (DF < 1 and carry-over 1/2), so the unbalanced moments shrink geometrically and the process converges.

questions.q: Fixed beam central load 60 kN, L 6 m: FEM
questions.why: FEM for a central load is WL/8 = 60 × 6/8 = 45 kN·m.

questions.q: Propped cantilever UDL 10 kN/m, L 8 m: fixed moment
questions.why: The fixed-end moment of a propped cantilever with UDL is wL²/8 = 10 × 64/8 = 80 kN·m.

questions.q: Fixed beam with support sinking 10 mm, EI 2×10⁴ kN·m², L 5 m: induced end moments
Case: Beam ABC (A fixed, C pinned), AB 4 m, BC 4 m, EI constant. DF at B for BA and BC
questions.why: With A fixed, k_BA = 4EI/4 = EI. With C pinned, k_BC = 3EI/4 = 0.75EI. DF_BA = 1/1.75 = 0.571 and DF_BC = 0.75/1.75 = 0.429.

Portal (pinned bases) with 30 kN lateral load, h 5 m: column top moment
questions.why: The 30 kN lateral load is shared by the two columns, 15 kN each. A pinned-base column of height 5 m has a top moment of 15 × 5 = 75 kN·m.

questions.q: Max sagging moment of propped cantilever with UDL
questions.why: For a propped cantilever with UDL the maximum sagging moment is 9wL²/128, at 3L/8 from the prop.
The mid-span deflection of a fixed beam with central load is WL³/(192EI), a quarter of the simply supported value WL³/(48EI).

steps.title: Determinacy, cables, arches
steps.body:
- Truss D_s = m + r − 2j; frames D_s = 3m + r − 3j − c
- Cable H = wL²/8d; T_max = √(H² + V²); length ≈ L + 8d²/3L
- Arch: H from crown M = 0; M = M_beam − Hy; parabolic UDL ⇒ M = 0

steps.title: Deflection
steps.body:
- Moment-area: Δθ = area of M/EI; deviation = first moment
- Conjugate: slope = shear, deflection = moment; fixed ↔ free
- Unit load: δ = ∫Mm/EI; trusses ΣPuL/AE
- Castigliano δ = ∂U/∂P; least work ∂U/∂R = 0; Maxwell δ_ij = δ_ji

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: A simply supported beam has 3 reactions and 3 equations, so D_s = 0 (determinate).
A cable is flexible and carries load only by tension.
Moment-area Theorem I gives the change of slope between two points as the area of the M/EI diagram between them.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Real fixed end becomes in conjugate beam
quiz.why: In the conjugate beam method, a fixed end of the real beam becomes a free end in the conjugate beam.

quiz.q: Mock 1: ILD for R_A at A
quiz.why: With the unit load at A, all of it is carried by support A, so the ILD ordinate of R_A at A is 1.
For a fixed beam with a central point load, the FEM is WL/8.
For a prismatic member the carry-over factor is 0.5, so half of the applied moment appears at the far fixed end.
The slope-deflection method uses joint rotations and sway as unknowns, since it is a displacement method.

questions.why: If D_s < 0 the structure has too few restraints, so it is unstable (a mechanism).

questions.q: Conjugate beam shear equals real beam
questions.why: In the conjugate beam method the shear in the conjugate beam equals the slope of the real beam, and its moment equals the deflection.

questions.q: ILD for BM at C has a peak of
questions.why: The peak ordinate of the bending moment ILD at C is ab/L.
A fixed end cannot rotate, so its distribution factor is zero.

questions.q: Fixed beam UDL mid-span moment, w 10, L 6
questions.why: Mid-span moment of a fixed beam with UDL = wL²/24 = 10 × 36/24 = 15 kN·m.

questions.q: Max BM at 2 m section of 10 m span for 50 kN
Prop reaction, propped cantilever UDL 12 kN/m, 6 m
questions.why: The prop reaction of a propped cantilever with UDL is 3wL/8 = 3 × 12 × 6/8 = 27 kN.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Müller-Breslau principle gives the ILD as a deflected shape.  Reason (R): By Betti's theorem the deflected shape after releasing the restraint is proportional to the influence function.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: by Betti's reciprocal theorem the deflected shape after releasing the restraint is proportional to the influence function. That is the basis of the Müller-Breslau principle, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Arch L 24, h 6, point load 60 kN at 6 m from A: H
questions.why: V_B = 60 × 6/24 = 15 kN. Moments about the crown for the right half: V_B × 12 = H × 6, so H = 30 kN.

questions.q: Truss joint deflection Σ PuL = 360 kN·m, AE = 1.8×10⁵ kN
Cantilever 2 m, UDL 18 kN/m, EI 12 000 kN·m²: tip deflection
Moment distribution: A fixed, B joint, C fixed; AB 6 m UDL 20 kN/m, BC 3 m unloaded, EI const. DF_BA
questions.why: With A fixed, k_BA = 4EI/6 = 0.667EI and with C fixed, k_BC = 4EI/3 = 1.333EI. DF_BA = 0.667/2 ≈ 0.333.

questions.q: Unbalanced moment at B for that beam (FEM_BA = +60)
questions.why: The unbalanced moment at a joint is the sum of the fixed-end moments there. With FEM_BA = +60 kN·m and nothing on the other side in this beam, the unbalanced moment is 60 kN·m (wL²/12 = 60).

questions.q: Case: Final M_AB for that beam after one cycle (carry-over from BA distribution of −20)
questions.why: The unbalanced −20 at B is distributed in ratio of stiffness: −20 to BA and −40 to BC (per the beam's distribution factors). Half of the BA moment is carried over to A: −10. So M_AB = −60 − 10 = −70 kN·m.

questions.q: Two 80 kN loads 3 m apart on 15 m span: absolute max BM
questions.why: For two equal loads W at spacing x, M_max = W(L − x/2)²/(2L) = 80 × (15 − 1.5)²/30 = 80 × 182.25/30 = 486 kN·m.

questions.q: Propped cantilever central load: prop reaction for W = 32 kN
questions.why: For a propped cantilever with central load, the prop reaction is 5W/16 = 5 × 32/16 = 10 kN.

questions.q: Portal frame with 3 members, 4 joints, both bases fixed (r = 6), rigid joints: D_s
questions.why: For a rigid-jointed plane frame D_s = 3m + r − 3j = 9 + 6 − 12 = 3, so it is indeterminate to degree 3.

courses.summary: Soil formation and types, three-phase diagram and weight–volume relations, specific gravity, density, void ratio, porosity, degree of saturation, relative density, grain-size analysis (sieve and hydrometer), Atterberg limits and indices, and the Indian Standard soil classification system.

scenes.text: A lab receives a wet soil sample from a building site.
Weighing it wet and dry gives everything needed for phase relations.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Water content w = W_w/W_s; void ratio e = V_v/V_s; porosity n = V_v/V = e/(1 + e); degree of saturation S = V_w/V_v.
Key relations: Se = wG; γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e) = γ/(1 + w); γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e); γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w; γ_bulk = (G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e).
Air content a_c = V_a/V_v; percentage air voids n_a = n·a_c.
Relative density D_r = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Water content relative to total weight (it's relative to dry solids).
- Using n and e interchangeably.
- Forgetting γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³ (or 10 if the problem says so).

activity.prompt: Saturated soil: w = 30%, G = 2.65. Void ratio e?

quiz.why: The fundamental relation of soil mechanics is S e = w G: degree of saturation × void ratio = water content × specific gravity of solids.
Porosity n = V_v/V and e = V_v/V_s. Since V = V_s(1 + e), n = e/(1 + e).
Dry unit weight γ_d = weight of solids/total volume = Gγ_w/(1 + e).

quiz.q: Water content is defined relative to
quiz.why: Water content is the weight of water divided by the weight of solids (dry weight), not the total weight, so it can exceed 100%.
A relative density of 80% falls in the 65–85% range, which is called dense. Below 15% is very loose, and above 85% very dense.

scenes.text: An earth dam's filter must stop fine soil washing out but still drain.
Grain-size curves tell how well-graded each material is.

steps.title: Tests and coefficients
steps.body:
Sieve analysis for coarse soil (> 75 µm); hydrometer (sedimentation, Stokes' law) for fines.
D₁₀ (effective size), D₃₀, D₆₀ from the curve. Uniformity coefficient C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀; coefficient of curvature C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀D₆₀).
Well-graded gravel: C_u > 4, 1 ≤ C_c ≤ 3; well-graded sand: C_u > 6, 1 ≤ C_c ≤ 3. Uniform (poorly graded) soils have C_u near 1; gap-graded have C_c outside the range.
IS sizes: gravel 80–4.75 mm, sand 4.75–0.075 mm, silt 0.075–0.002 mm, clay < 0.002 mm.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** D₁₀ = 0.15, D₃₀ = 0.40, D₆₀ = 1.2 mm: C_u = 8, C_c = 0.16/0.18 = 0.89 ⇒ C_c < 1 ⇒ poorly graded sand (SP).

**Example 2.** D₁₀ = 0.1, D₃₀ = 0.35, D₆₀ = 0.8: C_u = 8, C_c = 1.53 ⇒ well-graded sand (SW).

**Example 3.** Stokes: particle 0.01 mm, G = 2.7, μ = 0.001 Pa·s: v = (2.7 − 1)(9810)(10⁻⁵)²/(18 × 0.001) = 9.3×10⁻⁵ m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading D₁₀ as the 10th sieve rather than the 10% finer size.
- Applying gravel criteria to sand.
- Hydrometer results without dispersing agent.

activity.prompt: D₁₀ = 0.2 mm, D₆₀ = 1.4 mm. Uniformity coefficient?

quiz.why: The coefficient of uniformity is C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀, which indicates the spread of grain sizes.
A soil is well graded when the coefficient of curvature C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀D₆₀) lies between 1 and 3 (and C_u is large enough).
In IS classification sand is 4.75 mm to 0.075 mm. Gravel is larger and silt/clay smaller.
Hydrometer analysis finds the size of fine particles from their settling speed in water, using Stokes' law.
The effective size is D₁₀, the diameter below which 10% of the soil is finer (used in Hazen's formula).

scenes.text: Houses on black cotton soil in central India crack as the soil swells and shrinks.
Atterberg limits predict that behaviour.

steps.title: Limits and indices
steps.body:
Liquid limit w_L (Casagrande cup: 25 blows), plastic limit w_P (3 mm thread crumbles), shrinkage limit w_S.
Plasticity index I_P = w_L − w_P; liquidity index I_L = (w − w_P)/I_P; consistency index I_C = (w_L − w)/I_P = 1 − I_L.
Activity A = I_P/(% clay fraction < 2 µm): inactive < 0.75, normal 0.75–1.25, active > 1.25 (montmorillonite highly active).
Flow index I_f = slope of water content vs log(blows); toughness index I_T = I_P/I_f.
Shrinkage limit (from dry pat): w_S = (V_d/W_d − 1/G)γ_w × 100 (method dependent).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** w_L = 60%, w_P = 25%, w = 40%: I_P = 35; I_L = 0.43; I_C = 0.57 (stiff-ish).

**Example 2.** I_P = 35, clay fraction 25% ⇒ A = 1.4 (active — likely expansive).

**Example 3.** Natural w > w_L ⇒ I_L > 1 ⇒ very soft, may behave like a liquid when disturbed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping liquid and plastic limits.
- Using total fines instead of < 2 µm clay fraction for activity.
- Interpreting negative I_L as an error (it means the soil is drier than the plastic limit — stiff).

activity.prompt: w_L = 48%, w_P = 22%, natural w = 35%. Liquidity index?

quiz.why: Plasticity index I_P = w_L − w_P, the water content range over which the soil is plastic.

quiz.q: Liquid limit cup test standard blows
quiz.why: In the Casagrande cup test the liquid limit is the water content at which the groove closes in 25 blows.
Skempton's activity A = plasticity index/clay fraction (% finer than 2 μm).
Montmorillonite has a weak, water-absorbing structure and is highly expansive. Kaolinite is much less so, and illite is intermediate.
Consistency index I_C = (w_L − w)/I_P and liquidity index I_L = (w − w_P)/I_P. Adding gives (w_L − w_P)/I_P = 1.

scenes.text: A geotechnical report labels a soil 'CH' — highly plastic clay.
IS 1498 uses grain size and the plasticity chart.

steps.title: IS 1498 system
steps.body:
Coarse-grained: > 50% retained on 75 µm. Gravel (G) if > half of coarse fraction retained on 4.75 mm, else sand (S). Suffix W/P (well/poorly graded, if fines < 5%), M/C (silty/clayey fines, if fines > 12%), dual symbols for 5–12%.
Fine-grained: > 50% passes 75 µm. Plasticity chart: A-line I_P = 0.73(w_L − 20). Above A-line ⇒ clay (C); below ⇒ silt (M); organic (O). Compressibility: L (w_L < 35), I (35–50), H (> 50).
Peat (Pt) — highly organic.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 70% passing 75 µm, w_L = 55, I_P = 30: A-line value 0.73 × 35 = 25.6 < 30 ⇒ above ⇒ CH.

**Example 2.** w_L = 40, I_P = 8: A-line 14.6 > 8 ⇒ below ⇒ MI.

**Example 3.** 60% sand, 35% gravel, 5% fines, C_u = 8, C_c = 1.5 ⇒ SW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 50% instead of the IS boundaries (35/50) for compressibility.
- Forgetting the A-line equation.
- Classifying coarse soils without checking fines percentage.

activity.prompt: Classify (IS 1498)

quiz.why: On the plasticity chart, the A-line is I_P = 0.73(w_L − 20). Soils above it are clays, and those below are silts or organic soils.
A soil is fine-grained when more than 50% passes the 75 μm sieve.
In IS classification, high compressibility (H) means w_L > 50%; intermediate (I) is 35–50% and low (L) is below 35%.

quiz.q: Dual symbols used when fines are
quiz.why: Dual symbols (such as SW-SM) are used when the fines are between 5% and 12%.
Pt is the symbol for peat and other highly organic soils.

questions.why: Void ratio is volume of voids over volume of solids, which can exceed 1, as it commonly does for soft clays and organic soils.
In IS classification, clay-size particles are smaller than 0.002 mm.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A soil with natural water content above its liquid limit has I_L > 1.  Reason (R): I_L = (w − w_P)/(w_L − w_P) exceeds 1 when w > w_L.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: I_L = (w − w_P)/(w_L − w_P) is greater than 1 when w > w_L, so the soil is in a liquid state. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Degree of saturation: w 20%, G 2.7, e 0.72

questions.why: A = I_P/clay fraction = 20/40 = 0.5. Values below 0.75 are inactive.

questions.q: Case: A site soil has w_L 52, I_P 32, 85% fines. IS symbol
questions.why: Fines are more than 50%, and w_L > 50 means high compressibility. The A-line at w_L = 52 is 0.73 × 32 = 23.4. Since I_P = 32 is above it, the soil is a clay, so CH.
Air voids as a fraction of the total volume = n(1 − S) = 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.08 = 8%.

questions.q: Wet mass 1.9 kg, dry 1.6 kg, V 1000 cm³, G 2.7: e

courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 2 · Permeability, seepage and effective stress
courses.summary: Darcy's law, permeability tests (constant head, falling head, pumping), factors affecting k, equivalent permeability of layered soils, effective stress principle, seepage pressure and quick sand, flow nets and seepage discharge, and capillarity in soils.
outcomes: Compute k from lab and field tests
Find equivalent permeability of layered deposits
Apply σ′ = σ − u with and without seepage
Use flow nets for seepage and check against piping (quick condition)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A basement excavation fills with groundwater.
How fast water seeps depends on the soil's permeability k.

steps.title: Darcy and tests
steps.body:
Darcy: v = ki (laminar), q = kiA. Seepage velocity v_s = v/n.
- Constant head (coarse soils): k = QL/(Aht).
- Falling head (fine soils): k = (aL/(At)) ln(h₁/h₂) = 2.303(aL/(At)) log₁₀(h₁/h₂).
- Field pumping (unconfined): k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(π(h₂² − h₁²)); confined: k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πb(h₂ − h₁)).
Typical k (m/s): gravel 10⁻² +, sand 10⁻³–10⁻⁵, silt 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸, clay < 10⁻⁹.
Hazen: k (cm/s) ≈ C D₁₀² (D₁₀ in cm, C ≈ 100).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Constant head: Q = 500 cm³ in 100 s, L = 20 cm, A = 50 cm², h = 40 cm: k = 500 × 20/(50 × 40 × 100) = 0.05 cm/s.

**Example 2.** Falling head: a = 1 cm², A = 50 cm², L = 10 cm, h from 100 to 50 cm in 600 s: k = (1 × 10/(50 × 600)) ln 2 = 2.31×10⁻⁴ cm/s.

**Example 3.** Hazen: D₁₀ = 0.2 mm = 0.02 cm ⇒ k ≈ 100 × 0.0004 = 0.04 cm/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln vs log₁₀ without the 2.303 factor.
- Using discharge velocity as the actual velocity (divide by n).
- Applying Darcy's law to turbulent flow in coarse gravels.

activity.prompt: Constant head test: Q = 300 cm³ in 60 s, L = 15 cm, A = 30 cm², h = 25 cm. k (cm/s)?

quiz.why: Darcy's law says discharge velocity is proportional to the hydraulic gradient: v = ki.
The falling head test is used for fine-grained soils, where k is low and flow is too slow for a constant head test.
Seepage velocity is the real water velocity through the pores: v_s = v/n, larger than the discharge velocity.
Clays have very small pores, and their permeability is very low, below about 10⁻⁹ m/s.
Hazen's formula k = C·D₁₀² uses the effective size D₁₀.

lessons.title: Layered soils and factors affecting permeability

scenes.text: A site has sand, clay and silt layers one above another.
Water moves far more easily along the layers than across them.

steps.title: Equivalent permeability
steps.body:
Flow parallel to layers: k_h = Σkᵢ Hᵢ/ΣHᵢ (weighted mean).
Flow perpendicular: k_v = ΣHᵢ/Σ(Hᵢ/kᵢ) (harmonic-type mean).
Always k_h ≥ k_v. Factors: grain size (k ∝ D²), void ratio (k ∝ e³/(1 + e) — Kozeny–Carman), fluid viscosity (temperature), soil structure, degree of saturation, entrapped air.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Layers: 2 m sand (k = 10⁻⁴ m/s), 1 m clay (10⁻⁸), 2 m silt (10⁻⁶).
k_h = (2×10⁻⁴ + 10⁻⁸ + 2×10⁻⁶)/5 = 4.04×10⁻⁵ m/s.
k_v = 5/(2/10⁻⁴ + 1/10⁻⁸ + 2/10⁻⁶) = 5/(2×10⁴ + 10⁸ + 2×10⁶) = 4.9×10⁻⁸ m/s — controlled by the clay.

**Example 2.** Temperature: k₂₀ = k_T μ_T/μ₂₀ — warmer water flows more easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the formulas for horizontal and vertical flow.
- Ignoring a thin clay layer (it dominates vertical flow).
- Mixing units of k between layers.

activity.prompt: Two layers 1 m each with k = 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁶ m/s. Vertical equivalent k (×10⁻⁶ m/s, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: For flow parallel to the layers, the equivalent k_h = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i, a thickness-weighted average dominated by the most permeable layer.
For flow perpendicular to layers (in series), the least permeable layer controls the equivalent k_v.
In stratified soils k_h ≥ k_v, because horizontal flow follows the most permeable layers whereas vertical flow is held back by the least permeable.

quiz.q: k depends on grain size as
quiz.why: Permeability depends on the square of the grain (pore) size, k ∝ D², as in Hazen's and Poiseuille's equations.
A warmer fluid is less viscous, so water flows more easily and k increases with temperature.

lessons.title: Effective stress, seepage pressure and quick sand

scenes.text: Behind a cofferdam, sand suddenly boils up like porridge.
Upward seepage reduced effective stress to zero — quick condition.

steps.title: Effective stress
steps.body:
σ′ = σ − u (Terzaghi). Strength and compressibility depend on σ′.
Saturated soil (no flow) at depth z below water table: σ′ = γ′z.
Upward seepage (gradient i): σ′ = (γ′ − iγ_w)z; downward: (γ′ + iγ_w)z. Seepage force per unit volume j = iγ_w.
Quick condition: σ′ = 0 ⇒ critical gradient i_c = γ′/γ_w = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1. Factor of safety against piping = i_c/i_exit (≥ 3–4 recommended).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Clay γ_sat = 20 kN/m³, water table at surface, depth 5 m: σ = 100, u = 49.05, σ′ = 50.95 kPa.

**Example 2.** Sand G = 2.65, e = 0.65: i_c = 1.65/1.65 = 1.0. Exit gradient 0.25 ⇒ FS = 4.

**Example 3.** Lowering the water table by pumping increases σ′ ⇒ settlement of nearby buildings (a real risk in cities).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total stress for strength calculations.
- Forgetting u = 0 above the water table (ignoring capillarity unless stated).
- Sign of seepage effect (upward reduces σ′).

activity.prompt: Sand: G = 2.68, e = 0.68. Critical hydraulic gradient (2 decimals)?

quiz.why: Terzaghi's effective stress is σ′ = σ − u: total stress minus pore pressure.
Quick condition occurs when upward seepage force cancels the soil's submerged weight, so σ′ = 0 and the soil loses strength.
The critical gradient is i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e), where the effective stress becomes zero.
Downward seepage adds to the soil's weight (seepage force acts down), so effective stress is larger.
Seepage force per unit volume is j = iγ_w.

lessons.title: Flow nets and seepage under structures

scenes.text: Water seeps under a concrete weir from upstream to downstream.
A flow net gives the seepage quantity and the uplift pressures.

steps.title: Flow nets
steps.body:
Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles forming curvilinear squares (isotropic soil). Seepage q = kH(N_f/N_d) per unit width (N_f flow channels, N_d potential drops, H head loss).
Pore pressure at a point = γ_w × (total head − elevation head). Uplift on structures from equipotentials; exit gradient at the toe = Δh/l (Δh = H/N_d, l = last square size).
Anisotropic soil: transform x by √(k_v/k_h); use k′ = √(k_h k_v).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H = 6 m, N_f = 4, N_d = 12, k = 10⁻⁵ m/s: q = 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 4/12 = 2×10⁻⁵ m³/s/m = 1.73 m³/day/m.

**Example 2.** Exit square size 1 m: Δh = 0.5 m ⇒ i_exit = 0.5; with i_c = 1 ⇒ FS = 2 (inadequate — add a cut-off or filter).

**Example 3.** Anisotropic k_h = 9×10⁻⁶, k_v = 10⁻⁶: k′ = 3×10⁻⁶ m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting flow lines instead of flow channels.
- Using elevation head as pressure head.
- Ignoring anisotropy in transformed sections.

activity.prompt: Flow net: H = 8 m, N_f = 3, N_d = 12, k = 2×10⁻⁶ m/s. Seepage q (×10⁻⁶ m³/s per m)?

quiz.q: Flow lines and equipotentials meet at
quiz.why: Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles, which follows from Laplace's equation.
Seepage per unit width is q = k H (N_f/N_d), where N_f is the number of flow channels and N_d the number of potential drops.
The exit gradient is checked against the critical gradient to guard against piping (progressive erosion at the downstream end).
To draw the flow net for anisotropic soil, the section is transformed so that the equivalent permeability is √(k_h k_v).
Total head = elevation head + pressure head (+ velocity head, neglected), so the pressure head is total head − elevation head.

questions.why: Darcy's law is valid only for laminar flow, where velocity is proportional to gradient. It fails in turbulent flow.
Effective stress controls soil strength and volume change (compressibility), which is the basis of soil behaviour.
Clays have very low permeability because their pores are tiny.

questions.q: Falling head k: a 0.5 cm², A 20 cm², L 8 cm, h 60→30 in 300 s
σ′ at 4 m in saturated sand γ_sat 19 (water at surface)
questions.why: With water at the surface, σ′ = 4 × (γ_sat − γ_w) = 4 × (19 − 9.81) = 36.8 kPa.

questions.q: Seepage velocity for v = 10⁻⁴ m/s, n = 0.4
Assertion (A): A thin clay seam drastically reduces vertical permeability of a stratified deposit.  Reason (R): Vertical equivalent k is dominated by the least permeable layer.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: in vertical flow the layers are in series, so the equivalent permeability is controlled by the least permeable layer, and a thin clay seam cuts k_v sharply. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: σ′ with upward seepage i = 0.4 at 3 m (γ′ = 10 kN/m³)
FS against piping: i_c 1.05, exit gradient 0.35
Case: A cofferdam flow net has H = 5 m, N_f = 5, N_d = 10, k = 5×10⁻⁵ m/s, wall length 40 m. Daily inflow
Unconfined pumping: q = 0.01 m³/s, r₁ 10 m (h₁ 8 m), r₂ 50 m (h₂ 9 m)
questions.why: For unconfined flow, k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(π(h₂² − h₁²)) = 0.01 × ln 5/(π × 17) = 0.01 × 1.609/53.4 ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
Hazen: k = C D₁₀² with D₁₀ in cm: 100 × (0.01)² = 0.01 cm/s.

questions.q: Head needed for quick condition in 0.5 m thick sand (i_c 1) with upward flow
questions.why: Quick condition needs i = i_c = 1, and i = h/L, so h = i_c × L = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 m.
For vertical flow, k_v = ΣH/Σ(H/k) = 2/(1/10⁻⁴ + 1/10⁻⁸) = 2/(10⁴ + 10⁸) ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁸ m/s, controlled by the tight layer.

courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 3 · Compaction and consolidation
courses.summary: Compaction: Proctor tests, OMC and MDD, zero air voids line, field compaction and control; consolidation: one-dimensional theory, oedometer test, compression and swelling indices, normally and overconsolidated clays, settlement computation, Terzaghi's time factor and coefficient of consolidation.
outcomes: Interpret compaction curves, OMC, MDD and ZAV line
Specify and check field compaction
Compute primary consolidation settlement for NC and OC clays
Use time factor to estimate consolidation time
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A highway embankment is built in 300 mm layers compacted by rollers.
The lab Proctor test sets the target density and moisture.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Compaction = densification by expelling air (not water). Standard Proctor (2.6 kg rammer, 310 mm drop, 3 layers × 25 blows) vs modified Proctor (4.9 kg, 450 mm, 5 layers × 25) — higher energy ⇒ higher MDD, lower OMC.
Dry density ρ_d = ρ/(1 + w). Zero-air-voids line: ρ_d = Gρ_w/(1 + wG) (S = 1); line for air content n_a: ρ_d = (1 − n_a)Gρ_w/(1 + wG).
Dry of optimum: flocculated structure, higher strength, more swelling; wet of optimum: dispersed, more compressible, less permeable (clay cores of dams).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Mould 1000 cm³, wet mass 2.05 kg, w = 15%: ρ = 2.05 g/cc; ρ_d = 1.783 g/cc.

**Example 2.** ZAV at w = 15%, G = 2.7: ρ_d = 2.7/(1 + 0.405) = 1.922 g/cc.

**Example 3.** Relative compaction: field ρ_d 1.75, lab MDD 1.85 ⇒ 94.6% (specs often require ≥ 95% — re-roll).

steps.title: Field compaction
steps.body: Equipment: smooth-wheel rollers (granular base), sheepsfoot (clays), pneumatic-tyred (mixed soils), vibratory rollers/plates (sands). Control: core cutter or sand replacement for field density; nuclear gauges; moisture by rapid methods. Layer thickness and passes trial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking compaction removes water.
- Compacting far wet of optimum (pore pressure, pumping).
- Using wet density instead of dry density for relative compaction.

activity.prompt: Wet density 2.1 g/cc at w = 12%. Dry density (g/cc, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Compaction densifies soil by mechanical energy, which expels air from the voids (not water).
Modified Proctor uses more compactive energy, so it gives a higher maximum dry density at a lower optimum moisture content.
The zero-air-voids line is ρ_d = Gρ_w/(1 + wG), obtained by putting S = 1.
Sheepsfoot rollers use kneading action, which suits cohesive soils (clays). Clean sands use vibratory rollers.
Relative compaction is the field dry density divided by the laboratory maximum dry density.

scenes.text: The Tower of Pisa leans because the clay beneath one side consolidated more.
Consolidation is slow squeezing of water out of saturated clay under load.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
Load on saturated clay is first carried by pore water (excess pore pressure), which dissipates as water drains, transferring load to the soil skeleton. Primary consolidation (drainage), secondary compression (creep).
Oedometer: incremental loading, e vs log σ′ plot.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.body:
Coefficient of compressibility a_v = −Δe/Δσ′; m_v = a_v/(1 + e₀) (coefficient of volume change).
Compression index C_c = Δe/Δlog σ′ (virgin line); swelling/recompression index C_r ≈ C_c/5–C_c/10.
Empirical: C_c ≈ 0.009(w_L − 10) (Skempton, undisturbed NC clay).
Preconsolidation pressure σ′_c (Casagrande construction). OCR = σ′_c/σ′₀ (NC: 1; OC > 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using natural log in C_c (it's log₁₀).
- Ignoring preconsolidation (OC clays settle much less).
- Confusing consolidation (time-dependent drainage) with compaction (air expulsion).

activity.prompt: w_L = 60%. Skempton C_c = 0.009(w_L − 10)?

quiz.why: The compression index C_c is the slope of the e–log σ′ line: Δe/Δlog σ′.
Overconsolidation ratio OCR = preconsolidation pressure/present effective stress. For a normally consolidated clay these are equal, so OCR = 1.
Primary consolidation is the gradual squeezing out of pore water under load, which transfers load from pore pressure to the soil skeleton.
The coefficient of volume compressibility is m_v = a_v/(1 + e₀).
Casagrande's graphical construction on the e–log σ′ curve finds the preconsolidation pressure.

scenes.text: A warehouse on a 6 m soft clay layer is expected to settle.
Engineers compute settlement from C_c, e₀ and the stress increase.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
NC clay: S = [C_cH/(1 + e₀)] log₁₀((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀).
OC clay, σ′₀ + Δσ ≤ σ′_c: S = [C_rH/(1 + e₀)] log((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀).
OC clay, σ′₀ + Δσ > σ′_c: S = [H/(1 + e₀)][C_r log(σ′_c/σ′₀) + C_c log((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′_c)].
Alternatively S = m_v Δσ H. Use σ′₀ and Δσ at the mid-depth of the layer (or sub-layers).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** NC clay H = 4 m, e₀ = 1.0, C_c = 0.3, σ′₀ = 60 kPa at mid-depth, Δσ = 40 kPa: S = (0.3 × 4/2) log(100/60) = 0.6 × 0.2218 = 0.133 m.

**Example 2.** Same clay but OC with σ′_c = 120 kPa, C_r = 0.05: S = (0.05 × 4/2) log(100/60) = 0.022 m.

**Example 3.** m_v = 5×10⁻⁴ m²/kN, Δσ = 50 kPa, H = 3 m ⇒ S = 0.075 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using surface stress instead of mid-depth stress.
- Applying C_c to the recompression part.
- Forgetting (1 + e₀) in the denominator.

activity.prompt: NC clay: C_c 0.4, H 3 m, e₀ 1.2, σ′₀ 50 kPa, Δσ 50 kPa. Settlement (m, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: For normally consolidated clay the settlement is S = [C_c H/(1 + e₀)] log[(σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀], so C_c is used.
Stresses are computed at the mid-depth of the clay layer as an average representative value.
For overconsolidated clay when the final stress stays below the preconsolidation pressure, only the recompression index C_r is used.
Settlement using m_v is S = m_v Δσ H, a linear relation.
Overconsolidated clay is stiffer on the recompression branch, so for the same load it settles less than normally consolidated clay.
options: less than NC clays for the same load

scenes.text: A port reclamation on clay might take years to settle.
Vertical drains shorten the drainage path and speed it up dramatically.

steps.title: Terzaghi's theory
steps.body:
∂u/∂t = c_v ∂²u/∂z². Time factor T_v = c_v t/H_d² (H_d = drainage path: half thickness for double drainage, full thickness for single).
U ≤ 60%: T_v = (π/4)U². U > 60%: T_v = 1.781 − 0.933 log₁₀(100 − U%). T₅₀ = 0.197, T₉₀ = 0.848.
c_v from lab: Casagrande log-time (t₅₀) or Taylor √t (t₉₀). Also c_v = k/(m_v γ_w).
Prefabricated vertical drains and preloading accelerate consolidation (radial drainage).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Clay 6 m, double drainage (H_d = 3 m), c_v = 3 m²/yr: time for 90%: t = 0.848 × 9/3 = 2.54 years.

**Example 2.** Same clay single drainage (H_d = 6 m): t = 0.848 × 36/3 = 10.2 years (4×).

**Example 3.** Lab: 20 mm sample double drained (H_d = 10 mm), t₅₀ = 5 min ⇒ c_v = 0.197 × 100/5 = 3.94 mm²/min.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full thickness for double drainage.
- Mixing units of c_v (mm²/min vs m²/yr).
- Forgetting time scales with H_d².

activity.prompt: T_v for U = 50% using (π/4)U² (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: The time factor is T_v = c_v t/H_d², where H_d is the drainage path length.

quiz.q: Doubling drainage path multiplies time by
quiz.why: t ∝ H_d², so doubling the drainage path makes the time four times longer.
For 90% consolidation the time factor T₉₀ ≈ 0.848.
Vertical drains provide short horizontal drainage paths for pore water, which speeds up consolidation greatly.
The coefficient of consolidation is c_v = k/(m_v γ_w).

questions.why: Compaction expels air and rearranges the grains, which increases dry density (and lowers void ratio, permeability and compressibility).
Optimum moisture content (OMC) is the water content at which the soil attains maximum dry density for a given compactive effort.

questions.why: Secondary compression is the slow volume change that continues after pore pressures have dissipated, because of creep of the soil skeleton.

questions.why: For 90% consolidation the time factor is T_v ≈ 0.848.

options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false

courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 4 · Shear strength, earth pressure and bearing capacity
courses.summary: Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion, direct shear, triaxial (UU, CU, CD) and unconfined compression tests, sensitivity; Rankine's active and passive earth pressure with surcharge and water; Terzaghi's bearing capacity, factors of safety, and an introduction to settlement-based design and slope stability.
outcomes: Apply τ_f = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ and interpret test results
Compute active and passive pressures and resultants
Use Terzaghi's bearing-capacity equation
Outline slope stability factor of safety
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: After heavy monsoon rain, a hillside road cutting slides.
Rising pore pressure cut the effective stress — and with it the shear strength.

steps.title: Criterion
steps.body:
τ_f = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ (effective stress). Failure plane inclined at θ = 45° + φ′/2 to the major principal plane.
σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45 + φ/2) + 2c tan(45 + φ/2).
Typical: dense sand φ′ 35–45°, loose sand 28–32°, NC clay c′ ≈ 0, φ′ 20–30°; undrained clay φ_u = 0, strength c_u.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body: Direct shear (box) — simple, fixed failure plane. Triaxial: UU (undrained, quick — short-term stability), CU (with pore pressure measurement ⇒ effective parameters), CD (slow, drained — long-term). Unconfined compression (UCS, σ₃ = 0): c_u = q_u/2. Sensitivity S_t = q_u(undisturbed)/q_u(remoulded). Vane shear in field for soft clays.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** c′ = 10 kPa, φ′ = 30°, σ′ = 100 kPa: τ_f = 10 + 57.7 = 67.7 kPa.

**Example 2.** CD test on sand (c = 0): σ₃ = 100, σ₁ = 300 kPa at failure ⇒ sin φ = (300 − 100)/(300 + 100) = 0.5 ⇒ φ = 30°.

**Example 3.** UCS q_u = 80 kPa ⇒ c_u = 40 kPa; remoulded q_u = 20 ⇒ S_t = 4 (sensitive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total-stress parameters for long-term drained problems.
- Taking the failure plane angle as 45° − φ/2 from the major principal plane.
- Ignoring pore pressure rise in undrained loading of saturated clay.

activity.prompt: Sand c = 0, φ = 35°, σ′ = 150 kPa. Shear strength (kPa, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: The Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion is τ = c + σ tan φ, where c is cohesion and φ the angle of internal friction.

quiz.q: Failure plane angle with major principal plane
quiz.why: In a soil specimen at failure the failure plane makes an angle 45° + φ/2 with the major principal plane.
In a UCS test σ₃ = 0 and φ = 0, so c_u = q_u/2, where q_u is the unconfined compressive strength.
Long-term stability needs drained conditions (excess pore pressures dissipated), so drained (CD or effective-stress) parameters are used.
With c = 0, sin φ = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃) = 200/400 = 0.5, so φ = 30°.

scenes.text: A basement wall holds back soil and groundwater.
The soil pushes with active pressure; soil in front resists with passive pressure.

steps.title: Formulas (smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill)
steps.body:
K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2); K_p = 1/K_a; K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ′ (at rest).
Active pressure p_a = K_aγz − 2c√K_a; resultant (c = 0) P_a = ½K_aγH² at H/3 from the base.
Surcharge q: uniform K_aq over depth (resultant K_aqH at H/2).
Submerged backfill: use γ′ for soil + full water pressure γ_wz.
Cohesive soil: tension crack depth z_c = 2c/(γ√K_a).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H = 6 m, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30° (K_a = 1/3): P_a = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 36 = 108 kN/m at 2 m above base.

**Example 2.** Add surcharge 20 kPa: extra 20/3 × 6 = 40 kN/m at 3 m ⇒ total 148 kN/m.

**Example 3.** Clay c = 15 kPa, φ = 0, γ = 18: z_c = 2 × 15/18 = 1.67 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using K_p for retained soil.
- Forgetting water pressure behind undrained walls (often doubles the load — provide drainage).
- Taking the resultant at H/2 for triangular pressure.

activity.prompt: φ = 30°, γ = 20 kN/m³, H = 3 m, c = 0. Active thrust P_a (kN/m)?

quiz.q: Resultant of triangular active pressure acts at
quiz.why: Active pressure is triangular, and its resultant acts at H/3 above the base (the centroid of the triangle).
Jaky's equation gives the at-rest coefficient K₀ = 1 − sin φ for normally consolidated soil.
Drainage behind a wall reduces water pressure, which is often a large part of the lateral load.

scenes.text: A two-storey house column carries 600 kN to a footing on sandy clay.
Terzaghi's equation gives the ultimate bearing capacity.

steps.title: Terzaghi (general shear)
steps.body:
Strip: q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ (q = γD_f).
Square: 1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.4γBN_γ; circular: 1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.3γBN_γ.
φ = 0 (clay): N_c = 5.7, N_q = 1, N_γ = 0 ⇒ q_u = 5.7c + γD_f (Terzaghi); Skempton for clays N_c = 5 (1 + 0.2D/B)(1 + 0.2B/L) ≤ 7.5–9.
Safe bearing capacity q_s = (q_u − γD_f)/FS + γD_f (FS ≈ 3). Water table at base: use γ′ in the 0.5γBN_γ term.
Local shear (loose soils): use c′ = 2c/3, tan φ′ = (2/3)tan φ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Strip footing B = 2 m, D_f = 1 m, γ = 18, c = 0, φ = 30° (N_q = 22.5, N_γ = 19.7): q_u = 18 × 22.5 + 0.5 × 18 × 2 × 19.7 = 405 + 354.6 = 759.6 kPa; q_s = (759.6 − 18)/3 + 18 = 265 kPa.

**Example 2.** Square footing on clay c_u = 50 kPa, D_f = 1.5 m, γ = 18: q_u = 1.3 × 50 × 5.7 + 27 = 397.5 kPa.

**Example 3.** Column 600 kN, q_s = 200 kPa ⇒ area ≥ 3 m² ⇒ 1.75 m square.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shape factors for strip vs square.
- Not reducing γ for a high water table.
- Ignoring settlement criteria (allowable pressure may be governed by settlement, not shear).

activity.prompt: Clay c_u = 40 kPa, strip footing, D_f = 1 m, γ = 18. Terzaghi q_u = 5.7c + γD_f (kPa)?

quiz.why: Terzaghi's equation for a strip footing is q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ.
For φ = 0 (undrained clay), N_q = e^(π tan φ) tan²(45° + φ/2) = 1 × 1 = 1, while N_γ = 0 and N_c is about 5.14–5.7.
The shape factor for the cohesion term of a square footing is 1.3 (and 0.8 for the γ term).

quiz.q: Water table at the base affects
quiz.why: A water table at the base reduces the unit weight in the N_γ term to the submerged weight γ′.
options: the γ in the N_γ term

quiz.q: Typical factor of safety on bearing capacity
quiz.why: A factor of safety of about 3 is typically applied to the ultimate bearing capacity.

lessons.title: Slope stability and foundation settlement basics

scenes.text: A hill road's embankment must not slip in monsoon.
Factor of safety compares available strength with mobilised stress.

steps.title: Infinite slopes and methods
steps.body:
Dry cohesionless infinite slope: FS = tan φ/tan β (β = slope angle).
With seepage parallel to slope: FS = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β) ≈ ½ the dry value.
Finite slopes: Swedish slip-circle (φ = 0: FS = c_u L_a R/(W x̄)), method of slices (Fellenius, Bishop), Taylor's stability number S_n = c/(F γ H).
Remedies: flatten slope, drainage, retaining structures, soil nailing, vegetation.

steps.title: Foundation settlement (brief)
steps.body: Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary. Immediate settlement S_i = qB(1 − ν²)I_f/E. Differential settlement causes cracking — limits set by codes (e.g. angular distortion ~1/300–1/500). Plate load and SPT tests are field tools for sands (N-value correlations).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Dry sand φ = 35°, slope β = 25°: FS = 0.700/0.466 = 1.50.

**Example 2.** Same slope with full parallel seepage, γ′/γ_sat = 10/20: FS = 0.75 (unsafe).

**Example 3.** Elastic settlement: q = 150 kPa, B = 2 m, E = 20 MPa, ν = 0.3, I_f = 1: S_i = 150 × 2 × 0.91/20 000 = 13.7 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring pore pressure in wet-season stability checks.
- Using total stress analysis for long-term slopes in clay.
- Confusing allowable bearing pressure (settlement-governed) with safe bearing capacity (shear-governed).

activity.label: Slope angle β for dry sand with φ = 35° (FS = tan φ/tan β)

bands.text: β > φ: FS < 1 — the slope will fail.

quiz.why: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope, FS = tan φ/tan β.

quiz.q: Parallel seepage reduces FS by about
quiz.why: With seepage parallel to the slope, the stabilising effective weight is reduced from γ_sat to γ′, so FS falls to about γ′/γ_sat ≈ half of the dry value.
Bishop's method divides the sliding mass into slices, so it is a method of slices for slope stability.
Total settlement is the sum of immediate (elastic), primary consolidation and secondary compression.
Taylor's stability number is N_s = c/(Fγ H), related to slope angle and depth factor.

questions.why: In an unconfined compression test there is no cell pressure, so σ₃ = 0.
Passive pressure is greater than active pressure because K_p > K_a.
Sensitivity is the ratio of undisturbed strength to remoulded strength at the same water content.

questions.q: Tension crack depth: c 20 kPa, γ 16, φ 0
questions.why: The depth of the tension crack is z_c = 2c/γ (for φ = 0) = 2 × 20/16 = 2.5 m.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Long-term stability of clay slopes should use effective stress parameters.  Reason (R): Excess pore pressures dissipate over time, so drained conditions govern.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: excess pore pressures dissipate over time, so in the long term drained (effective stress) conditions govern and effective-stress parameters are right. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Active thrust: H 5 m, γ 18, φ 30°, surcharge 10 kPa
questions.why: Soil thrust = ½K_aγH² = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 25 = 75 kN/m. Surcharge thrust = K_a q H = (1/3) × 10 × 5 = 16.7 kN/m. Total ≈ 91.7 kN/m.

questions.q: Submerged backfill (γ′ 10), φ 30°, H 4 m, water to top: total thrust (soil + water)
questions.why: Soil thrust uses γ′: ½ × (1/3) × 10 × 16 = 26.7 kN/m. Water thrust = ½ × 9.81 × 16 = 78.5 kN/m. Total ≈ 105.2 kN/m.

questions.q: Case: A square footing 2 m on sand (c = 0, φ = 35°, N_q 41.4, N_γ 42.4), D_f 1 m, γ 18. q_u
questions.why: For a square footing on sand, q_u = qN_q + 0.4γBN_γ = 18 × 41.4 + 0.4 × 18 × 2 × 42.4 = 745 + 611 ≈ 1356 kPa.

questions.q: Safe bearing capacity for that case (FS 3)
questions.why: Safe bearing capacity q_s = (q_u − γD_f)/FS + γD_f = (1356 − 18)/3 + 18 = 446 + 18 ≈ 464 kPa.

Dry sand slope φ 32°, β 20°: FS
Footing area for 900 kN at q_s 250 kPa

quiz.q: Mock 1: Falling head test is for

Darcy's law holds for laminar flow, where v = ki.
