steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: h_L = K V²/(2g). Entrance (sharp) K = 0.5; exit loss = 1.0 (V²/2g); 90° bend K ≈ 0.9 (standard elbow ≈ 0.3–0.9); gate valve open ≈ 0.2. **Sudden expansion:** h_L = (V₁ − V₂)²/2g. **Sudden contraction:** h_L ≈ 0.5 V₂²/2g. Equivalent length L_e = K d/f.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring minor losses in short pipes.
- Using the wrong velocity (downstream for contractions).
- Not adding the exit loss.

lessons.title: Pipes in series and parallel; water hammer

scenes.text: A pump station valve closes in a second and a loud bang shakes the pipe: water hammer.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Series:** Q same, h_f adds. **Parallel:** h_f same, Q adds; with equal f: Q₁/Q₂ = √(d₁⁵ L₂/(d₂⁵ L₁)). Three-reservoir problem and loop networks (Hardy Cross: ΔQ = −Σh_f/(nΣ|h_f/Q|)). **Water hammer (Joukowsky):** Δp = ρ c ΔV for rapid closure (closure time < 2L/c); wave speed c = √(K/ρ)/√(1 + KD/(Et)), around 1000–1400 m/s in steel/ductile iron pipes. Control: slow valves, surge tanks, air vessels, relief valves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding heads in parallel (they are equal).
- Using closure time ≥ 2L/c with Joukowsky (it then over-predicts).
- Ignoring pipe elasticity in c.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: Free surface at atmospheric pressure; driving force is gravity. Uniform flow: S₀ = S_f = S_w. **Chezy:** V = C√(RS). **Manning (SI):** V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}; R = A/P. n: 0.011–0.013 smooth concrete, 0.015 rough concrete, 0.025 earth, 0.035 weedy. Q = AV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the free-surface width in the wetted perimeter.
- Using Manning n with US units.
- Using R = y for narrow channels only (wide-channel approximation).

story.title: Least excavation for a given flow

scenes.text: A canal contractor wants the cheapest section for a given discharge.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Results
steps.body: For given A, S, n, the section with maximum discharge has minimum wetted perimeter. **Rectangle:** b = 2y, R = y/2. **Trapezoid:** half of a regular hexagon: side slope 60° (1 V : 0.577 H), R = y/2. Semicircle is best overall. Practical sections also consider seepage, scour and economy.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Best rectangle with A = 8 m²: 2y² = 8 → y = 2 m, b = 4 m, R = 1 m. Manning n = 0.013, S = 0.0001: V = (1/0.013)(1)(0.01) = 0.769 m/s; Q = **6.15 m³/s**.

**Example 2.** Best trapezoid: R = y/2 for any size.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking b = y instead of b = 2y.
- Believing best section is cheapest in all cases (rock, shallow depth).
- Using total depth including freeboard.

lessons.title: Specific energy, critical depth and Froude number

scenes.text: A small bed hump in a channel makes the flow dip — or jump — depending on the regime.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **E = y + V²/2g = y + q²/(2gy²)** (rectangular, q = Q/b). Critical flow: dE/dy = 0 → **y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}**, E_min = 1.5 y_c, V_c = √(g y_c). **Froude** Fr = V/√(g D) (D = A/T): Fr < 1 subcritical (tranquil), = 1 critical, > 1 supercritical (rapid). Gradually varied flow profiles: M1, M2, S1, S2… classified by bed slope and depth relative to y_n and y_c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Q instead of q = Q/b.
- Applying the rectangular formula to trapezoidal channels.
- Mixing up sub- and supercritical when sketching profiles.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: Momentum balance for a rectangular channel: **y₂/y₁ = ½(√(1 + 8Fr₁²) − 1)**. Energy loss **ΔE = (y₂ − y₁)³/(4 y₁ y₂)**. Types by Fr₁: 1–1.7 undular, 1.7–2.5 weak, 2.5–4.5 oscillating, 4.5–9 steady (best), > 9 strong. Length ≈ 6 y₂. Uses: stilling basins, energy dissipation, mixing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Bernoulli across the jump (energy is lost).
- Using Fr₂ in the formula for y₂ from y₁.
- Forgetting that jumps only form from supercritical to subcritical.

lessons.title: Impulse–momentum and force of a jet

scenes.text: Firefighters brace against the reaction of a high-pressure nozzle.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **F = ρ Q (V₂ − V₁)** (force on fluid). Jet on a fixed flat plate normal to it: F = ρ a V². On a moving plate (speed u): F = ρ a (V − u)²; for a series of plates: F = ρ a V (V − u). Fixed curved vane turned through 180°: F = 2ρ a V². Pipe bends: F_x, F_y from momentum plus pressure forces.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Jet d = 50 mm, V = 20 m/s: a = 0.0019635 m²; F = 1000×0.0019635×400 = **785.4 N** on a normal plate.

**Example 2.** The same jet reversed by a symmetrical vane: F = **1570.8 N**.

**Example 3.** Series of plates moving at u = 8 m/s: F = 1000×0.0019635×20×12 = **471 N**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that moving a single plate reduces the mass flow hitting it.
- Missing the pressure term on pipe bends.
- Sign errors in momentum change.

scenes.text: A 1:25 spillway model is built; engineers scale the results to the real dam.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Buckingham π:** n variables, m fundamental dimensions → (n − m) π-groups. Key groups: **Reynolds** ρVL/μ (viscous), **Froude** V/√(gL) (gravity, free surface), **Euler** p/ρV², **Mach** V/c, **Weber** ρV²L/σ. **Froude model (L_r = L_m/L_p):** V_r = √L_r, Q_r = L_r^{2.5}, T_r = √L_r, F_r = L_r³ (same fluid). Spillways, channels, ships, weirs use Froude modelling; pipes and submerged bodies use Reynolds.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1:25 spillway; Q_m = 0.02 m³/s → Q_p = 0.02×25^{2.5} = 0.02×3125 = **62.5 m³/s**; V_p = V_m×5; force scale 25³ = **15 625**.

**Example 2.** Model time 10 s → prototype time = 10×√25 = **50 s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Reynolds similarity for free-surface flow with the same fluid (impractical).
- Inverting the scale ratio.
- Forgetting that Q scales as L^{5/2} under Froude.

scenes.text: Silt of 0.1 mm settles slowly in a sedimentation tank — Stokes' law decides how slowly.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Boundary layer: thin region next to a surface where viscosity matters. Plate: Re_x = ρVx/μ; laminar for Re_x < 5×10⁵; δ = 5x/√Re_x (laminar). **Drag:** F_D = ½ρ C_D A V². **Stokes' law** (Re < 1): F = 3πμdV; terminal velocity v_s = g d²(ρ_s − ρ)/(18μ). Separation occurs under adverse pressure gradients; streamlining reduces pressure drag.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Stokes' law for Re > 1.
- Using diameter in mm.
- Using the wetted area instead of the projected area for bluff-body drag.

story.title: Selecting a pump for an overhead tank

scenes.text: A building needs 50 L/s lifted 30 m. What power and what happens if the speed changes?
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Centrifugal pump: impeller adds energy to the fluid; casing (volute) converts velocity head to pressure. **Hydraulic power** P = ρgQH; **shaft power** = ρgQH/η. **Affinity laws:** Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³ (same impeller). **NPSH_a ≥ NPSH_r** to avoid cavitation. Specific speed N_s = N√Q/H^{3/4}. Series pumps add heads; parallel add discharges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using P in kW with Q in L/s inconsistently.
- Ignoring cavitation margins.
- Applying affinity laws to different pumps.

activity.prompt: Q = 0.05 m³/s, H = 30 m, η = 0.7. Shaft power (kW)?

story.title: Choosing a turbine for a hill stream

scenes.text: A micro-hydro site drops 400 m with small flow; another has 20 m head and large flow.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: **Impulse turbine (Pelton):** high head (roughly above 250 m), low flow; jet velocity V = C_v√(2gH); bucket speed u ≈ 0.45 V. **Reaction turbines:** Francis (medium head, mixed flow), Kaplan (low head, large flow, adjustable blades). Power available P = ρgQH; overall efficiency η_o = shaft power/P. Draft tube recovers kinetic energy for reaction turbines. Governing, runaway speed and unit quantities used for selection.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gross head for net head (losses in penstock).
- Choosing Kaplan for high head.
- Confusing impulse (atmospheric runner) with reaction (pressure change).

items.q: Why is the venturimeter C_d near 0.98?
items.a: The smooth converging and diverging sections keep losses and separation very small.

items.q: Why does a hydraulic jump lose energy?
items.a: Turbulent mixing in the roller dissipates kinetic energy; Bernoulli cannot be applied across it.

items.q: Why are spillway models Froude-scaled?
items.a: Free-surface gravity-driven flow is governed by the ratio of inertia to gravity.

items.q: What is cavitation?
items.a: Vapour bubbles form where local pressure falls to vapour pressure and collapse violently, damaging pumps and turbines.

items.q: Why is the centre of pressure below the centroid?
items.a: Pressure grows with depth so the resultant acts deeper than the centroid.

questions.q: Jet force d=40 mm, V=12 m/s (N)
Assertion: Pumps cavitate if NPSHa < NPSHr. Reason: pressure falls to vapour pressure at the impeller eye.

uni-civil-geotech-1.title: Geotechnical Engineering I (Soil Mechanics)
uni-civil-geotech-1.description: Soil mechanics for B.Tech civil: phase relations, classification, permeability and seepage, effective stress, compaction, stress distribution, consolidation and shear strength, with solved numericals and standard soil-lab practicals. Independent study companion.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Soil formation, phase relations and classification
courses.summary: Three-phase diagram, unit weights, index properties, Atterberg limits, grain-size analysis and IS classification.
outcomes: Solve phase relation problems
Compute consistency indices
Interpret grain-size curves with Cu and Cc
Classify fine-grained soils using the plasticity chart

story.title: A bucket of black cotton soil

scenes.text: A site engineer weighs a field sample, dries it in an oven and weighs it again.
From three numbers she can derive void ratio, water content, unit weights and saturation.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Soil = solids + water + air. Void ratio **e = Vv/Vs**, porosity **n = Vv/V = e/(1+e)**, water content **w = Ww/Ws**, degree of saturation **S = Vw/Vv**, specific gravity **Gs = γs/γw** (typically 2.6–2.8).

Key identity: **S e = w Gs**.

steps.title: Unit weights
steps.body: Bulk γ = (Gs + S e)γw/(1+e); dry γd = Gs γw/(1+e); saturated γsat = (Gs + e)γw/(1+e); submerged γ' = γsat − γw. Take γw = 9.81 kN/m³.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Entering w and S as percentages inside formulae, and mixing γ with ρ (kg/m³ vs kN/m³).

activity.prompt: Gs = 2.65, e = 0.65, S = 1 (saturated). Find γsat in kN/m³ (γw = 9.81).

quiz.q: Identity linking w, Gs, S and e

scenes.text: A clay road is hard in summer, sticky after rain, and flows like soup in a flood.
The water contents at which behaviour changes are the Atterberg limits.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body:
- **Liquid limit (LL)**: water content at which soil flows (25 blows in Casagrande cup / 20 mm cone penetration in IS cone test).
- **Plastic limit (PL)**: rolls into 3 mm thread and crumbles.
- **Shrinkage limit (SL)**: volume stops reducing on drying.

PI = LL − PL; Liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI; consistency index CI = (LL − w)/PI; Activity A = PI/(% clay fraction); flow index = slope of flow curve; toughness index = PI/If.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: LL = 48 %, PL = 25 %, w = 32 %: PI = **23**; LI = (32 − 25)/23 = **0.30**; CI = (48 − 32)/23 = 0.70 (stiff-ish). LI between 0 and 1 means plastic state.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Soils with high PI swell and shrink; LI above 1 means the natural soil is wetter than its liquid limit and will collapse when disturbed (sensitive clays).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using LI formula with LL instead of PL, and forgetting that sands are non-plastic (NP).

activity.prompt: LL = 48, PL = 25, w = 32. Liquidity index?

scenes.text: A lab technician shakes sand through stacked sieves, then settles the fines in a jar.
The result is a smooth S-shaped grading curve.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: Coarse fraction (> 75 μm): sieve analysis. Fines: hydrometer or pipette using **Stokes' law** v = (γs − γw) D²/(18 μ). Report % finer vs log particle diameter. D10 = effective size.

steps.title: Coefficients
steps.body: **Cu = D60/D10**, **Cc = D30²/(D10 D60)**. Well-graded gravel: Cu > 4 and Cc 1–3; well-graded sand: Cu > 6 and Cc 1–3; otherwise poorly graded.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Reading D on a linear scale, and calling a soil well graded using only Cc.

quiz.q: Well graded sand needs Cu above

lessons.title: IS soil classification and plasticity chart

scenes.text: A borehole log needs a standard symbol so every engineer reads the same soil.
The plasticity chart assigns clay or silt names.

steps.title: IS 1498 scheme
steps.body: Coarse-grained: more than 50 % retained on 75 μm (G gravel, S sand; W/P/M/C modifiers). Fine-grained: more than 50 % passes 75 μm: classified by LL and PI on the plasticity chart: **L** (LL < 35), **I** (35–50), **H** (> 50). A-line: **PI = 0.73 (LL − 20)**. Above A-line = clay (C), below = silt (M) or organic (O).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: LL = 48, PI = 23: A-line PI = 0.73×28 = 20.4. Point lies above the A-line and LL is 35–50 → **CI** (clay of intermediate plasticity). If LL = 62 and PI = 30 (A-line 30.7) it lies just below → MH.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using PL on the horizontal axis, and ignoring the dual symbols (e.g. SW-SM) for 5–12 % fines.

activity.prompt: Match symbol and meaning

courses.title: Unit 2 · Permeability, seepage and effective stress
courses.summary: Darcy's law, permeability tests, flow nets, effective stress principle, capillarity and quick condition.
outcomes: Compute permeability from lab data
Draw conclusions from flow nets

scenes.text: Seepage beneath a small dam must be estimated.
A lab permeameter measures k for the soil.

steps.title: Darcy
steps.body: v = k i, Q = k i A, with i = Δh/L. Seepage velocity vs = v/n. Typical k: gravel > 10⁻² m/s, clean sand 10⁻⁵–10⁻³, silt 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁵, clay < 10⁻⁹ m/s.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body: Constant head: k = Q L/(A h t). Falling head: k = 2.303 (a L/(A t)) log10(h1/h2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using ln instead of log10 with the 2.303 factor, and confusing discharge velocity with seepage velocity.

activity.prompt: Constant head test: Q=100 cm³, L=15 cm, A=50 cm², h=30 cm, t=120 s. k in 10⁻³ cm/s?

scenes.text: A sheet pile wall cuts off seepage under a weir.
A flow net of curved squares shows how much leaks.

steps.title: Flow net
steps.body: Streamlines and equipotentials meet at right angles forming curvilinear squares. **q = k H Nf/Nd** per metre run, Nf = flow channels, Nd = equipotential drops. Exit gradient ie = (H/Nd)/(exit element length).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: k = 10⁻⁵ m/s, H = 6 m, Nf = 4, Nd = 10: q = 10⁻⁵×6×4/10 = **2.4×10⁻⁵ m³/s per m**. Head drop per drop = 0.6 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting flow lines instead of channels (channels = lines − 1), and ignoring anisotropy of k.

activity.prompt: k=1e-5 m/s, H=6 m, Nf=4, Nd=10. q in 10⁻⁵ m³/s per m?

scenes.text: An excavation near a river floor bubbled with sand at its base.
Water pressure had cancelled the soil's effective stress.

steps.title: Terzaghi
steps.body: **σ' = σ − u**. Strength and volume change depend on effective stress, not total stress. Total stress σ = Σ γ h; pore pressure u = γw hw below water table.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Water table at ground surface: sand 4 m (γsat = 19 kN/m³) over clay 3 m (γsat = 17). At 7 m: σ = 4×19 + 3×17 = 127 kPa; u = 7×9.81 = 68.7 kPa; **σ' = 58.3 kPa**.

steps.title: Quick condition
steps.body: Upward seepage: σ' = 0 when i = icr = (Gs − 1)/(1 + e). For Gs = 2.65, e = 0.65: icr = 1.65/1.65 = **1.0**. Safe exit gradient uses factor of safety 3–5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using γ' with u as well (double counting buoyancy), and forgetting capillary rise raises effective stress.

activity.prompt: Gs=2.65, e=0.65. Critical hydraulic gradient?

quiz.q: Effective stress at 7 m in example (kPa)

scenes.text: A road embankment compacted too wet developed ruts within weeks.
There is an optimum moisture content for density.

steps.title: Standard Proctor (IS 2720 Part 7)
steps.body: Rammer 2.6 kg, drop 310 mm, 3 layers × 25 blows, mould 1000 cm³. Modified Proctor: 4.9 kg, 450 mm drop, 5 layers × 25 blows. Plot γd vs w; peak gives **maximum dry density (MDD)** at **optimum moisture content (OMC)**. Modified test gives higher MDD, lower OMC.

steps.title: Zero-air-voids
steps.body: γd(zav) = Gs γw/(1 + w Gs) at S = 1. The compaction curve lies below it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Reporting wet density as dry density, and expecting the compaction curve to cross the ZAV line.

steps.title: Equipment
steps.body: Smooth-wheel rollers for gravel/sand and finishing; sheepsfoot (tamping) for clays; pneumatic-tyred for mixed soils; vibratory rollers for granular soils; rammers/plate compactors for trenches. Lift thickness about 150–300 mm.

steps.title: Control
steps.body: Field density by sand replacement (IS 2720-28), core cutter (fine soils), nuclear gauge. Specification typically ≥ 95–98 % of MDD at OMC ± 2 %.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using sheepsfoot rollers on clean sand, and lifts too thick for the roller energy.

story.title: How deep does a footing's load go?

scenes.text: A column footing loads the soil; a nearby pipe sits 3 m down.

steps.title: Boussinesq point load
steps.body: σz = (3Q/(2π z²)) [1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^(5/2). Directly below (r = 0): σz = 0.4775 Q/z². Assumes homogeneous, isotropic, elastic half space.

steps.title: Approximate 2:1 method
steps.body: Load spreads at 2 vertical : 1 horizontal: σz = Q/((B + z)(L + z)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the footing width where r is needed, and applying stress at the footing level instead of below it.

lessons.title: Terzaghi's theory and the oedometer test

story.title: The leaning tower and the sponge

scenes.text: Soft clay beneath a tower squeezed out water for decades, tilting it.
A sponge in a cylinder under a spring models the process.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: On loading saturated clay, the excess pore pressure initially carries all the load (Δu = Δσ). As water drains, load transfers to the skeleton: effective stress rises and the soil compresses. Time depends on low permeability.

steps.title: Oedometer
steps.body: A thin disc (e.g. 60 mm dia × 20 mm) is loaded in increments doubling every 24 h between porous stones. Gives e–log σ' curve, preconsolidation pressure σ'c (Casagrande), compression index Cc, coefficient of consolidation cv (square-root-time or log-time method), mv.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating consolidation as immediate settlement, and confusing it with compaction.

statements.s: At the instant of loading, excess pore pressure equals the applied stress.
Consolidation is the same as compaction.
statements.why: Consolidation is time-dependent drainage; compaction is by mechanical energy and air expulsion.

statements.s: Sands consolidate much faster than clays.

quiz.q: Initial Δu on loading saturated clay

scenes.text: A warehouse slab will add 50 kPa on a 4 m clay layer.
The designer needs the final settlement.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: Normally consolidated: Sc = Cc H/(1 + e0) log10((σ'0 + Δσ)/σ'0). Overconsolidated with σ'0 + Δσ ≤ σ'c: use Cs (swelling index, about Cc/5 to Cc/10) in place of Cc. Also Sc = mv Δσ H. Typical Cc ≈ 0.009 (LL − 10) (Terzaghi–Peck, remoulded clays).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using natural log, using σ' at the top of the layer, and applying Cc when the soil is overconsolidated.

activity.prompt: Settlement (mm) for H=4 m, e0=0.9, Cc=0.30, σ'0=80, Δσ=50 kPa

quiz.q: Sc for double H in example (mm)

scenes.text: The owner wants to know how many months until 50% settlement.
Time factor Tv links time, cv and drainage path.

steps.title: Time factor
steps.body: Tv = cv t/Hdr². Hdr = H for single drainage, H/2 for double drainage. For U < 60 %: **Tv = (π/4) U²** (U as a fraction). Tv = 0.197 at 50 %, 0.848 at 90 %.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 4 m clay between sand layers (double drainage): Hdr = 2 m, cv = 10⁻⁷ m²/s. U = 50 %: Tv = (π/4)(0.5)² = 0.196. t = 0.196×4/10⁻⁷ = 7.85×10⁶ s = **90.9 days**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using H instead of Hdr, and entering U as a percentage in the formula.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Plot e vs log σ'. The straight virgin part slope is Cc = Δe/log10(σ2'/σ1'). Casagrande: find point of max curvature, draw horizontal, tangent, bisector; intersection with virgin line gives σ'c.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Shear strength of soils
courses.summary: Mohr–Coulomb criterion, Mohr circle, direct shear, triaxial and unconfined tests, drainage conditions.

Compute φ from direct shear data

scenes.text: After monsoon rain a cut slope failed along a plane.
Shear strength is a friction law on effective stress.

steps.title: Law
steps.body: τf = c' + σ'n tan φ'. Cohesion c' (clays) and friction φ' (sands, gravels have c = 0). Failure when the Mohr circle touches the envelope; failure plane angle θ = 45° + φ/2 from the major principal plane.

steps.title: Principal stresses at failure
steps.body: σ1 = σ3 tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2). Equivalent: σ1 = σ3 Nφ + 2c √Nφ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using σ instead of σ' in drained analysis, and measuring failure plane angle from the wrong plane.

activity.prompt: σ3 = 100 kPa, φ = 30°, c = 20 kPa. σ1 at failure (kPa)?

quiz.q: Failure plane angle with major plane

scenes.text: A split box holds a sand specimen under a normal load.
The upper half is pushed until the soil shears.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 60×60 mm box. Apply normal stress σ, shear at constant rate, record peak shear force. Repeat at 3 normal stresses; plot τ vs σ; slope = φ, intercept = c. Simple, quick, but drainage not controlled and failure plane forced.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: σ = 100 kPa gives τf = 70 kPa for dry sand: tan φ = 0.70 → φ = **35.0°**. Three tests: σ = 50, 100, 150 and τ = 40, 75, 110 kPa: slope = 70/100 = 0.7 → φ = 35°, intercept c = 40 − 35 = **5 kPa**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using too fast a shearing rate in clays (excess pore pressure), and plotting force instead of stress.

activity.prompt: Dry sand: σ = 100 kPa, τf = 70 kPa. φ in degrees?

scenes.text: A storage tank will be filled fast on soft clay.
The engineer needs undrained strength, so UU triaxial.

steps.title: Triaxial
steps.body: Cylindrical specimen (38 mm dia × 76 mm) in a cell: confining σ3 plus axial deviator. Types: **UU** (undrained, no consolidation) for short-term; **CU** with pore pressure measurement for effective parameters; **CD** drained for long term. For saturated clay UU: φu = 0, cu = (σ1 − σ3)/2.

steps.title: Unconfined compression
steps.body: σ3 = 0: qu = 2cu for saturated clay. Consistency: qu < 25 kPa very soft, 25–50 soft, 50–100 medium, 100–200 stiff. Sensitivity St = qu(undisturbed)/qu(remoulded).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: qu = 120 kPa → cu = **60 kPa**. Remoulded qu = 30 kPa → St = **4**. UU: σ3 = 100, σ1 = 220 → cu = 60 kPa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using UU parameters for long-term stability; quoting qu rather than cu in bearing capacity.

activity.prompt: UCS test: qu = 120 kPa. Undrained cohesion cu?

steps.title: Phase and index

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions

items.q: Why is effective stress important?
items.a: Strength and compressibility of soil depend on stress carried by the grains, σ' = σ − u, not total stress.

items.q: Why does a high PI matter?
items.a: It signals large volume change and low strength on wetting; such soils need special treatment.

items.q: Why compaction on the wet side of optimum?
items.a: Gives a dispersed structure with lower permeability and better flexibility, useful for clay liners and cores.

items.q: When do we use UU vs CD?

items.q: What is preconsolidation pressure?

story.title: The warehouse that was built before the borings

scenes.text: A developer started pouring footings before any soil data existed; a buried clay pocket cost three months.
A proper investigation would have mapped it for a fraction of the cost.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
1. Desk study and reconnaissance (geology, maps, nearby records).
2. Preliminary investigation (few boreholes, geophysics).
3. Detailed investigation (boreholes, sampling, in-situ and lab tests).
4. Reporting with recommendations.

Purpose: soil profile, ground-water level, strength, compressibility, hazards (fill, expansive soil, liquefaction).

steps.title: Depth and spacing (IS 1892 guidance)
steps.body: Explore to the depth where the stress increase falls to about 10 % of the foundation pressure (roughly 1.5 B for an isolated footing, about 3 B or more for a raft). Spacing depends on variability: about 30–50 m for uniform sites, closer for erratic ones; at least one boring to a competent stratum for every important structure.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A 24 m × 12 m building on isolated footings of B = 2.5 m: depth ≈ 1.5×2.5 ≈ 3.75 m below founding level. If founding at 1.5 m, the boring depth is about 5.5 m minimum, extended if soft strata persist.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Stopping borings in a soft layer, and ignoring the ground-water level fluctuation.

steps.title: Methods of boring
steps.body: Auger boring (shallow, above water), wash boring, percussion, rotary drilling (rock/coring), test pits for shallow depth. Samples: **disturbed** (representative, for classification) and **undisturbed** (for strength and consolidation, thin-walled Shelby tube or piston sampler).

steps.title: Area ratio
steps.body: Ar = (Do² − Di²)/Di² × 100 %. For good undisturbed sampling Ar should be small (about 10 % or less). Inside clearance Cr = (Ds − De)/De with Ds = inside diameter of tube, De = diameter of cutting edge (typically 0.5–3 %).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Do = 52 mm, Di = 50 mm: Ar = (2704 − 2500)/2500 = **8.2 %** — acceptable. A split-spoon with Do = 50.8, Di = 35: Ar = (2580.6 − 1225)/1225 = 111 % — only a disturbed sample.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling SPT split-spoon samples undisturbed, and driving thin-wall tubes with hammer blows.

steps.title: Interpretation (Terzaghi–Peck)
steps.body: Sand: N 0–4 very loose, 4–10 loose, 10–30 medium, 30–50 dense, > 50 very dense. Clay: N < 2 very soft, 2–4 soft, 4–8 medium, 8–15 stiff, 15–30 very stiff, > 30 hard. Corrections: overburden (sand), hammer energy and rod length, dilatancy for fine saturated sand: N' = 15 + ½(N − 15) for N > 15.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Raw N = 31 in saturated fine sand below WT: N' = 15 + 0.5×(31 − 15) = **23**. Medium dense — much less than the raw 'dense' reading.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Counting the seating 150 mm blows in N, and applying the dilatancy correction to clays.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Bearing capacity of shallow foundations
courses.summary: Failure modes, Terzaghi and general bearing capacity equations, water table, safe bearing pressure and plate load test.
outcomes: Apply Terzaghi's equation
Use bearing capacity factors with shape and depth
Correct for water table

lessons.title: Failure modes and Terzaghi's bearing capacity

scenes.text: A grain silo on soft clay rotated and lifted soil on one side — a classic base failure.
Terzaghi's theory predicts the ultimate pressure before that happens.

steps.title: Failure modes
steps.body: **General shear** (dense sand, stiff clay: distinct failure surface and heave), **local shear** (medium), **punching shear** (loose/soft: no heave). Ultimate bearing capacity qu is the pressure at which the soil fails; net ultimate qnu = qu − γDf.

steps.title: Terzaghi's equations
steps.body:
Strip: qu = c Nc + q Nq + 0.5 γ B Nγ.
Square: qu = 1.3 c Nc + q Nq + 0.4 γ B Nγ.
Circular: qu = 1.3 c Nc + q Nq + 0.3 γ B Nγ.
q = γ Df. For φ = 30°: Nc = 37.2, Nq = 22.5, Nγ = 19.7; φ = 0: Nc = 5.7, Nq = 1, Nγ = 0. Local shear uses c* = 2c/3 and tan φ* = 2/3 tan φ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using c in the Nc term for pure sand, and applying FS to gross qu without adding back overburden consistently.

activity.prompt: Terzaghi strip footing: q=27 kPa, Nq=22.5, γ=18, B=2, Nγ=19.7, c=0. qu in kPa?

story.title: A real footing is not a strip

scenes.text: Footings are rectangular, embedded and sometimes loaded at an angle.
Shape, depth and inclination factors adjust the strip result.

steps.title: Form
steps.body: qu = c Nc sc dc ic + q Nq sq dq iq + 0.5 γ B Nγ sγ dγ iγ Rw. Meyerhof-type factors: Nq = e^(π tanφ) tan²(45° + φ/2), Nc = (Nq − 1) cot φ, Nγ = (Nq − 1) tan(1.4φ). For φ = 30°: **Nq = 18.40, Nc = 30.14, Nγ = 15.67**. Water table correction: Rw ≈ 0.5 when WT is at or above the base, 1.0 if at depth ≥ B below base.

steps.title: Water table
steps.body: If the WT is at the base, use γ' (= γsat − γw) in the γB term (the surcharge term keeps γ above WT). If WT is at ground level both terms use γ'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing factor tables from different authors in one calculation, and applying Rw and γ' together (double reduction).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Safe bearing capacity qs = qnu/FS + γDf (FS typically 2.5–3). Allowable bearing pressure also limits settlement. Eccentric load: q(max,min) = Q/(BL) (1 ± 6e/B); no tension if **e ≤ B/6** (middle third).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Letting e exceed B/6 without redistributing (the formula then gives tension), and omitting footing self-weight.

story.title: A 300 mm plate in a pit

steps.title: IS 1888 procedure
steps.body: Excavate to founding level; place a 300–750 mm square plate on a levelled bed; load in increments (about 1/5 of design load), hold until settlement rate < 0.02 mm/min, read dial gauges; continue to failure or 1.5× design load. For sand: Sf = Sp [Bf(Bp + 0.3)/(Bp(Bf + 0.3))]²; qf ≈ qp (Bf/Bp) for sand; for clay qf = qp (width independent).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Plate Bp = 0.3 m settles 10 mm at design pressure. Footing Bf = 2 m: ratio = (2×0.6)/(0.3×2.3) = 1.739; squared = 3.02; **Sf = 30.2 mm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Extrapolating plate results below depth of influence of the plate (about 2 Bp) and ignoring layered soil.

steps.title: Components
steps.body: Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary compression. In sands immediate settlement dominates.

steps.title: Elastic formula
steps.body: Si = q B (1 − μ²) If / Es, where If = influence factor depending on shape/rigidity, Es = soil modulus (kPa), μ = Poisson's ratio.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using total instead of net pressure, and ignoring that Es increases with depth.

steps.title: Limits (IS 1904 typical)
steps.body: Isolated footings: sand about 50 mm, clay about 75 mm; rafts: sand about 75 mm, clay about 100 mm total; differential limits are smaller (angular distortion about 1/500 for framed buildings with brittle finishes). Always check the current code.

steps.title: Footing selection
steps.body:
- **Isolated**: single column, adequate soil.
- **Combined / strap**: close columns or property-line columns.
- **Strip**: walls or rows of columns.
- **Raft/mat**: footings cover more than about 50 % of plan area; reduces differential settlement; floating raft when excavated soil weight ≈ building weight.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Checking only bearing capacity and not settlement, and ignoring adjacent foundation interference.

scenes.text: A 600 kN column and a 400 kN column are 4 m apart.
The footing must be centred on the resultant to give uniform pressure.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Total load Q = Q1 + Q2 (+ self-weight allowance).
2. Locate resultant: x = Q2 s/(Q1 + Q2) from column 1.
3. Footing length L = 2(x + distance from column 1 to the near end).
4. Width B = Q/(L qa).
5. Design as an inverted beam (moment and shear diagrams).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Q1 = 600, Q2 = 400, s = 4 m: Q = 1000 kN; x = 400×4/1000 = **1.6 m** from column 1. If the footing extends 0.5 m beyond column 1: L = 2(1.6 + 0.5) = 4.2 m. For qa = 150 kPa: B = 1000/(4.2×150) = **1.59 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Centring the footing on the mid-point of columns instead of the resultant.

scenes.text: A bridge pier needs to bypass 15 m of soft alluvium.
The contractor weighs driven versus bored piles.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body: By function: **end-bearing** (rest on hard stratum) and **friction** (shaft resistance). By material: timber, steel, concrete (precast, cast in situ), composite. By installation: driven, bored cast in situ, driven cast in situ. By displacement: displacement piles vs non-displacement (bored).

steps.title: Practical points
steps.body: Driven piles densify sand but vibrate and cause heave; bored piles suit congested sites, need stabilisation (bentonite or casing) and clean base. Minimum spacing ≈ 2.5–3 d (friction piles 3 d, end-bearing 2 d).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using driven piles near vibration-sensitive structures, and ignoring bentonite cake effects on shaft friction.

lessons.title: Static capacity of a single pile

scenes.text: A 400 mm bored pile goes 12 m into clay with cu = 50 kPa.

steps.title: General
steps.body: Qu = Qp + Qs. Allowable Qa = Qu/FS (FS ≈ 2.5). Clay (total stress, α-method): Qp = 9 cu Ap, Qs = α cu As, α ≈ 0.5–1.0 (about 0.7 typical for bored piles in medium clay). Sand: Qp = q Nq Ap, Qs = K σ'v tanδ As.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using perimeter of pile at tip area, and counting full shaft in the top fill that will settle (negative skin friction).

lessons.title: Pile groups and negative skin friction

scenes.text: A pier is carried by a 3×3 pile group under a cap.
Fill placed after piling drags down on the shafts.

steps.title: Group efficiency
steps.body: Converse–Labarre: η = 1 − θ/90 · [(n − 1)m + (m − 1)n]/(m n), θ = tan⁻¹(d/s) in degrees, m rows, n columns. Group capacity = η × (number of piles) × single-pile capacity, or block failure of the soil mass — take the lesser.

steps.title: Negative skin friction
steps.body: When soil around a pile settles more than the pile (new fill on soft clay), downward drag adds load on the pile. Estimate Qn = α cu As over the settling length; reduce with bitumen coating.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming η > 1 for piles in clay, and ignoring drag-down in reclaimed land.

steps.title: Procedure (IS 2911 Part 4)
steps.body: Install test pile and reaction system (kentledge or anchor piles); place jack and dial gauges; apply maintained load in increments of 20 % of the design (safe) load; hold each until settlement rate is below 0.1 mm/h (or time limit); load to 2× design load; unload; plot load–settlement. Safe load is the lesser of ½ the load for the stated settlement criterion or two-thirds of the load for a specified net settlement.

scenes.text: A basement wall bulged after a drain clogged.
Lateral pressure grows with depth and with water.

steps.title: Coefficients
steps.body: Active Ka = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ) = tan²(45° − φ/2); passive Kp = 1/Ka; at rest K0 ≈ 1 − sinφ. For φ = 30°: Ka = 1/3, Kp = 3, K0 = 0.5. Cohesive soil: σa = Ka γ z − 2c√Ka; tension crack depth zc = 2c/(γ√Ka).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
H = 5 m, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30°, c = 0: pressure at base = (1/3)×18×5 = 30 kPa; **Pa = ½ Ka γ H² = 0.5×(1/3)×18×25 = 75 kN/m**, acting at H/3 = **1.667 m** above base.
Clay φ = 0, c = 20, γ = 18: zc = 2×20/18 = **2.22 m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting hydrostatic pressure of water behind the wall, and using Kp as the allowable resistance without a safety margin.

lessons.title: Coulomb theory and design of gravity walls

scenes.text: A 5 m gravity wall holds back a road embankment.
The engineer checks overturning, sliding and bearing.

steps.title: Coulomb
steps.body: Coulomb's wedge theory accounts for wall friction δ and wall inclination, giving Ka slightly lower than Rankine for rough walls; thrust is inclined at δ to the normal.

steps.title: Stability checks
steps.body: FS overturning = ΣMr/ΣMo ≥ 2; FS sliding = μ ΣW/ΣPh ≥ 1.5; bearing pressure within qa with resultant in the middle third (e ≤ B/6).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
W = 200 kN/m acting 1.5 m from the toe, Pa = 75 kN/m at 1.667 m. Mo = 75×1.667 = 125 kNm; Mr = 200×1.5 = 300 kNm → FS = **2.4** OK.
Sliding with μ = 0.5: 0.5×200/75 = **1.33 < 1.5** — fails: add a shear key or widen the base.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Neglecting drainage behind the wall (weep holes, filter) and adding passive resistance of soil that may be removed.

scenes.text: A hill road cutting failed after three days of heavy rain.

steps.title: Infinite slope (cohesionless)
steps.body: Dry: FS = tanφ/tanβ. With seepage parallel to slope: FS ≈ (γ'/γsat) tanφ/tanβ (about half). Failures: translational, rotational (circular), compound.

steps.title: Finite slopes
steps.body: Taylor stability number Sn = c/(F γ H) read from charts as a function of slope angle and φ. Method of slices (Fellenius): F = Σ(c l + N tanφ)/Σ T.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ignoring rain-induced pore pressure and using peak strength on a previously slipped slope (use residual).

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions

items.q: Why check settlement as well as bearing capacity?
items.a: Soil can be safe against shear failure yet settle enough, especially differentially, to damage the structure.

items.q: What is the middle-third rule?
items.a: The resultant must lie within B/3 of the base centre so the whole base stays in compression.

items.q: Why are piles used?
items.a: To bypass weak strata, resist uplift or lateral loads, or support heavy structures on poor shallow soils.

items.q: Why is Kp mobilised only partly?
items.a: Large wall movement is needed to reach full passive pressure; design uses a factor of safety.

items.q: What is negative skin friction?
